statements.quote: Before asking whether machines can *think*, it helps to ask what *reasoning* is in the first place.
statements.section: What is Reason?

statements.quote: The \citetitle{wikipedia_reason} (\citeyear{wikipedia_reason}) gives a working definition that has barely changed since Aristotle: **Reason** is the capacity to consciously apply logic by drawing valid conclusions from new or existing information, with the aim of seeking truth.
statements.section: What is Reason?

statements.quote: Three things make this definition load-bearing for the rest of this chapter:
statements.section: What is Reason?

statements.quote: The \citetitle{wikipedia_reason} (\citeyear{wikipedia_reason}) identifies four classical forms, all of which show up in modern AI:
statements.section: Forms of Logical Reasoning

statements.quote: | Form | Pattern | Example in AI |
statements.section: Forms of Logical Reasoning

statements.quote: | **Deductive** | General premises → necessary conclusion | A theorem prover: given axioms, derive the theorem.
statements.section: Forms of Logical Reasoning

statements.quote: | **Inductive** | Specific cases → probable generalisation | A model trained on millions of cat photos concludes “cats have fur.” |
statements.section: Forms of Logical Reasoning

statements.quote: | **Abductive** | Observation → best explanation | A doctor sees symptoms and infers the most likely disease.
statements.section: Forms of Logical Reasoning

statements.quote: Chain-of-thought prompting (see the Reasoning chapter ) blends all four: it decomposes a problem (deductive), appeals to patterns seen in training (inductive), proposes candidate answers (abductive), and maps structure across domains (analogical).
statements.section: Forms of Logical Reasoning

statements.quote: Three classical tensions run through the philosophy of reason and matter for AI:
statements.section: Reason vs. Emotion, Faith, and Truth

statements.quote: The field of **automated reasoning** studies how reasoning may or may not be modeled computationally.
statements.section: Automated Reasoning

statements.quote: Classical AI took this literally, hand-coded logic, theorem provers, expert systems.
statements.section: Automated Reasoning

statements.quote: Modern AI takes it *statistically*, the same four forms above, learned rather than programmed.
statements.section: Automated Reasoning

statements.quote: The shift from formal to statistical reasoning is arguably the single most important philosophical change of the deep-learning era, and it is what the rest of this textbook is about.
statements.section: Automated Reasoning

statements.quote: I believe that in about fifty years' time it will be possible to programme computers [...] to make them play the imitation game so well that an average interrogator will not have more than 70 percent chance of making the right identification after five minutes of questioning.
statements.section: The Turing Test: Performance vs. Presence

statements.quote: The **Turing Test**, originally proposed by Alan Turing in 1950 as the “Imitation Game,” was designed to bypass the messy question of “Can machines think?” by asking “Can machines *act* like they think?”
statements.section: The Turing Test: Performance vs. Presence

statements.quote: Historically, the Turing Test was the “holy grail” of AI.
statements.section: The Turing Test: Performance vs. Presence

statements.quote: Today, LLMs often pass informal Turing-style tests.
statements.section: The Turing Test: Performance vs. Presence

statements.quote: They can mimic the cadence, humor, and even the “errors” of human speech so effectively that a human judge can no longer reliably distinguish between silicon and soul in a text-based chat.
statements.section: The Turing Test: Performance vs. Presence

statements.quote: However, passing the test only proves **functional mimicry**, not **internal presence**.
statements.section: The Turing Test: Performance vs. Presence

statements.quote: It is comparatively easy to make computers exhibit adult level performance on intelligence tests or playing checkers, and difficult or impossible to give them the skills of a one-year-old when it comes to perception and mobility.
statements.section: Moravec's Paradox: The Hardship of the Simple

statements.quote: This is why we have AI that can pass the Bar Exam but we don't have a robot that can reliably clear a dinner table.
statements.section: Moravec's Paradox: The Hardship of the Simple

statements.quote: Evolution has “encoded” millions of years of sensorimotor optimization into our biology, making it feel “easy” to us, whereas abstract logic is a recent, thin veneer that is computationally easier to simulate with silicon.
statements.section: Moravec's Paradox: The Hardship of the Simple

statements.quote: In 1990 — building on his 1986 subsumption-architecture paper \citeauthorlastnameand{brooks1986layered} (\citeyear{brooks1986layered}) — roboticist \citeauthor{brooks1990elephants} (\citeyear{brooks1990elephants}) sharpened Moravec's empirical observation into a programmatic thesis.
statements.section: Brooks' Manifesto: "Elephants Don't Play Chess"

statements.quote: Where Moravec noted that sensorimotor skills are computationally hard, \citeauthor{brooks1990elephants} argued that the discipline's whole research agenda had been pointed at the wrong end of the problem.
statements.section: Brooks' Manifesto: "Elephants Don't Play Chess"

statements.quote: When we examine very simple level intelligence we find that explicit representations and models of the world simply get in the way.
statements.section: Brooks' Manifesto: "Elephants Don't Play Chess"

statements.quote: It is better to use the world as its own model.
statements.section: Brooks' Manifesto: "Elephants Don't Play Chess"

statements.quote: The title is the argument in miniature: elephants have huge brains, display sophisticated behaviour in their environment, and *do not play chess*.
statements.section: Brooks' Manifesto: "Elephants Don't Play Chess"

statements.quote: Yet for thirty years the field's flagship goal had been a chess grandmaster.
statements.section: Brooks' Manifesto: "Elephants Don't Play Chess"

statements.quote: \citeauthor{brooks1990elephants}' diagnosis was that classical, *symbolic* AI — what he called "Good Old-Fashioned AI" (GOFAI) — was solving the wrong problem.
statements.section: Brooks' Manifesto: "Elephants Don't Play Chess"

statements.quote: It tried to build intelligence by stacking ever more elaborate symbolic representations and inference engines on top of one another, in the hope that reasoning alone would bootstrap its way to generality.
statements.section: Brooks' Manifesto: "Elephants Don't Play Chess"

statements.quote: \citeauthor{brooks1990elephants}' counter-thesis, the seed of what became *nouvelle AI*, was that real-world competence comes from a creature's continuous sensorimotor coupling with its environment, not from detached symbol manipulation.
statements.section: Brooks' Manifesto: "Elephants Don't Play Chess"

statements.quote: He summarised the programme as eight claims, the most quoted of which read:
statements.section: Brooks' Manifesto: "Elephants Don't Play Chess"

statements.quote: The architectural consequence was the *subsumption architecture*: a layered stack of independently running, perception–action loops in which higher layers can subsume (override) the outputs of lower ones, without any central world model.
statements.section: Brooks' Manifesto: "Elephants Don't Play Chess"

statements.quote: Each layer is a thin, embodied competence (avoid obstacles, wander, explore, build maps, plan), wired directly from sensors to motors.
statements.section: Brooks' Manifesto: "Elephants Don't Play Chess"

statements.quote: There is no global representation, no explicit reasoning module, no place where a "central plan" lives.
statements.section: Brooks' Manifesto: "Elephants Don't Play Chess"

statements.quote: Brooks' robots — *Allen*, *Herbert*, *Genghis* — were built this way in the late 1980s and early 1990s, and they did navigate cluttered, dynamic environments.
statements.section: Brooks' Manifesto: "Elephants Don't Play Chess"

statements.quote: Crucially, they did so with what looked like no reasoning at all.
statements.section: Brooks' Manifesto: "Elephants Don't Play Chess"

statements.quote: The deeper point is *methodological*.
statements.section: Brooks' Manifesto: "Elephants Don't Play Chess"

statements.quote: \citeauthor{brooks1990elephants}' complaint was that symbolic AI was building systems that only worked in carefully constrained, sanitised worlds and failed the moment a camera frame shifted by one pixel.
statements.section: Brooks' Manifesto: "Elephants Don't Play Chess"

statements.quote: His alternative was to *build systems that work in the real world, with brittleness*, the right way to find out what we do not yet understand.
statements.section: Brooks' Manifesto: "Elephants Don't Play Chess"

statements.quote: The implicit wager was that progress comes from being forced to face the full mess of embodied reality, not from retreating into more abstract reasoning about an increasingly idealised one.
statements.section: Brooks' Manifesto: "Elephants Don't Play Chess"

statements.quote: The next historical root runs in a parallel direction.
statements.section: Maturana & Varela 1980: Autopoiesis — Life as a Self-Creating Process

statements.quote: While \citeauthor{brooks1990elephants} argued that *intelligence* is sensorimotor and embodied, two Chilean biologists working in Santiago had already argued, a decade earlier, that *life itself* — the biological substrate in which any embodied intelligence must run — is a peculiar kind of process: one that *produces and maintains itself*.
statements.section: Maturana & Varela 1980: Autopoiesis — Life as a Self-Creating Process

statements.quote: \citeauthor{maturana1980autopoiesis} (\citeyear{maturana1980autopoiesis}) named this process **autopoiesis** (Greek: *auto-* self + *poiesis* making) and proposed it as a precise definition of what makes a living system alive, distinguishing it sharply from an "allopoietic" system (one that produces something *other* than itself, like a factory) and from a trivial homeostatic loop (one that only stabilises a fixed variable).
statements.section: Maturana & Varela 1980: Autopoiesis — Life as a Self-Creating Process

statements.quote: An autopoietic machine is organized (defined as a unity) as a network of processes of production (transformation and destruction) of components which produce the components which: (i) through their interactions and transformations, continuously regenerate and realize the network of processes (relations) that produced them; and (ii) constitute it (the machine) as a concrete unity in the space in which it exists, by specifying the topological domain of its realization as a network.
statements.section: Maturana & Varela 1980: Autopoiesis — Life as a Self-Creating Process

statements.quote: The definition is dense and load-bearing.
statements.section: Maturana & Varela 1980: Autopoiesis — Life as a Self-Creating Process

statements.quote: Three ideas are smuggled into a single sentence.
statements.section: Maturana & Varela 1980: Autopoiesis — Life as a Self-Creating Process

statements.quote: First, an autopoietic system is *defined by its network of processes*, not by any particular material; the same autopoietic machine can swap out every molecule and remain "itself", so long as the network of processes that regenerate it stays intact — the Ship of Theseus, but stated as the *definition* of being alive rather than as a puzzle about identity.
statements.section: Maturana & Varela 1980: Autopoiesis — Life as a Self-Creating Process

statements.quote: Second, the network and its components are *mutually constitutive*: the components produce the network, and the network produces the components; the cell wall, the membrane, the ribosomes are themselves products of the cellular process they enable.
statements.section: Maturana & Varela 1980: Autopoiesis — Life as a Self-Creating Process

statements.quote: Third, the system *specifies its own boundary*: an autopoietic machine is the *thing* that draws the line between inside and outside, by producing the components that constitute the boundary.
statements.section: Maturana & Varela 1980: Autopoiesis — Life as a Self-Creating Process

statements.quote: Living systems are, on this definition, *closed networks of self-production* that *open up* an autonomous identity in a world they did not design.
statements.section: Maturana & Varela 1980: Autopoiesis — Life as a Self-Creating Process

statements.quote: A second move ties autopoiesis directly to cognition.
statements.section: Maturana & Varela 1980: Autopoiesis — Life as a Self-Creating Process

statements.quote: In the same book, Maturana and Varela argue that *cognition is the operation of an autopoietic system in its domain of interactions* — not "information processing about a world" but the *ongoing enactment* of a network that brings forth a world for itself by interacting with the medium.
statements.section: Maturana & Varela 1980: Autopoiesis — Life as a Self-Creating Process

statements.quote: This is the move that earns them the standard epithet "founders of the enactivist school of cognitive science", and it is precisely the move that ties their work to \citeauthor{brooks1990elephants}'s argument against disembodied AI.
statements.section: Maturana & Varela 1980: Autopoiesis — Life as a Self-Creating Process

statements.quote: Both Brooks and Maturana/Varela insist that intelligence is not the manipulation of abstract symbols over a pre-given world; it is what a body does, continuously, while staying alive.
statements.section: Maturana & Varela 1980: Autopoiesis — Life as a Self-Creating Process

statements.quote: The difference is one of *level*: Brooks is arguing about the *engineering* of intelligent robots ("don't try to play chess without a body"), while Maturana and Varela are arguing about the *biology* of cognition itself ("there is no cognition outside an autopoietic system").
statements.section: Maturana & Varela 1980: Autopoiesis — Life as a Self-Creating Process

statements.quote: The framing also gives a precise answer to a question that Brooks gestures at but does not pin down: *why does embodiment help?* The answer in the autopoietic vocabulary is that an embodied system is the only kind that has a *criterion of success* — staying alive, regenerating itself against perturbation.
statements.section: Maturana & Varela 1980: Autopoiesis — Life as a Self-Creating Process

statements.quote: An LLM has no such criterion; it has only a next-token probability distribution.
statements.section: Maturana & Varela 1980: Autopoiesis — Life as a Self-Creating Process

statements.quote: The "grounding problem" of the previous sections can be stated in this vocabulary as the absence of *autopoietic stakes*: there is no ongoing process that the model is responsible for keeping itself going, so there is no way for any of its outputs to count as *successful* in the sense that matters biologically.
statements.section: Maturana & Varela 1980: Autopoiesis — Life as a Self-Creating Process

statements.quote: Whether the cognitive science of the next century will develop a vocabulary for "non-autopoietic cognition" — cognition without biological self-maintenance — is open, but \citeauthor{maturana1980autopoiesis} have made the question *hard*: any such vocabulary must explain how a system can be said to *cognise* in the absence of any process whose continuation it is *responsible for*.
statements.section: Maturana & Varela 1980: Autopoiesis — Life as a Self-Creating Process

statements.quote: Five years before \citeauthor{mccullochpitts1943} (\citeyear{mccullochpitts1943}) published their logical-neuron paper, and eleven years before Hebb's learning rule, a young Spanish neuroanatomist named \citeauthor{lorentedeno1938cortex} (\citeyear{lorentedeno1938cortex}) — trained by Cajal in Madrid and then at the Rockefeller Institute — published a chapter in Fulton's *Physiology of the Nervous System* (1938) that would, in time, prove to be the missing anatomical link between the *cell* and the *mind*.
statements.section: Lorente de Nó 1938: Closed Loops Are the Brain's Computational Unit

statements.quote: The chapter's title is dry — \citetitle{lorentedeno1938cortex} — but the argument inside it is the first rigorous answer to a question that had been hanging over neuroscience since Sherrington: *how do billions of neurons wired together in a thin sheet of tissue give rise to anything at all?*
statements.section: Lorente de Nó 1938: Closed Loops Are the Brain's Computational Unit

statements.quote: The answer is two structural claims and one functional consequence.
statements.section: Lorente de Nó 1938: Closed Loops Are the Brain's Computational Unit

statements.quote: The **first structural claim** is that the cortex is built out of *vertical chains*: neurons are stacked through the cortical layers (II, III, IV, V, VI), each neuron's apical dendrite reaching up toward the pia, each neuron's axon projecting down or laterally, and the synaptic contacts between them densely populating the local vertical column.
statements.section: Lorente de Nó 1938: Closed Loops Are the Brain's Computational Unit

statements.quote: Lorente de Nó's micro-anatomy showed that the cortex is not the flat, undifferentiated sheet it had appeared in early Nissl images; it is a forest of *parallel vertical processing units*, each one a small column of cells tightly coupled, separated from its neighbours by sparser lateral connections.
statements.section: Lorente de Nó 1938: Closed Loops Are the Brain's Computational Unit

statements.quote: The **second structural claim** is that these chains are not simple feed-forward pipelines.
statements.section: Lorente de Nó 1938: Closed Loops Are the Brain's Computational Unit

statements.quote: The axon of each pyramidal cell sends out a *recurrent collateral* — a branch that loops back and re-enters the local chain, often within the same layer, often crossing several cells' dendrites on the way.
statements.section: Lorente de Nó 1938: Closed Loops Are the Brain's Computational Unit

statements.quote: The result, which Lorente de Nó states explicitly in the chapter, is that the cortical chains **contain closed loops**: "the chains include closed loops, as for example, 8-2, 18-8, or 8'-2', 25-8'".
statements.section: Lorente de Nó 1938: Closed Loops Are the Brain's Computational Unit

statements.quote: A diagram Lorente de Nó includes in the chapter, the famous *figure 66*, makes this concrete: a small pyramidal cell (8) sends its axon upward to synapse on a second cell (2), whose recurrent collateral returns to synapse again on cell (8), and from there the activity can either exit via an efferent fibre (ef) or re-circulate through the same loop.
statements.section: Lorente de Nó 1938: Closed Loops Are the Brain's Computational Unit

statements.quote: The "elementary cortical pattern" he derives is universal across the mammals he examined — mouse, cat, monkey, man — and is conserved through the elaboration of the cortex from mouse to human.
statements.section: Lorente de Nó 1938: Closed Loops Are the Brain's Computational Unit

statements.quote: The **functional consequence** is what made the chapter worth the rest of the century's work.
statements.section: Lorente de Nó 1938: Closed Loops Are the Brain's Computational Unit

statements.quote: If activity enters a closed loop of excitatory neurons, and if each pass through a synapse takes ~0.6 msec (Lorente de Nó's own measurement), then the loop can sustain *reverberatory activity* — a self-perpetuating pattern that keeps firing after the input has stopped, for as long as the synaptic weights and refractory periods keep the loop above threshold.
statements.section: Lorente de Nó 1938: Closed Loops Are the Brain's Computational Unit

statements.quote: Lorente de Nó writes: "each afferent impulse causes the cortical cells to be bombarded by a succession of impulses, thus creating in them a constant state of facilitation, and eventually stimulating them to discharge into their axons." The functional picture is exactly the one Hebb would publish in *The Organisation of Behaviour* eleven years later — "reverberatory circuits" as the substrate of *short-term memory*, with the persistent activity in the loop standing in for the remembered item — and the picture Hopfield would rediscover as the attractor dynamics of his 1982 network, with the loop replaced by a symmetric weight matrix but the *mathematical content* (fixed-point dynamics under a "Hebbian" outer-product rule) unchanged.
statements.section: Lorente de Nó 1938: Closed Loops Are the Brain's Computational Unit

statements.quote: Lorente de Nó is the *anatomical origin* of both ideas.
statements.section: Lorente de Nó 1938: Closed Loops Are the Brain's Computational Unit

statements.quote: The standard Anglophone history of neural networks skips this chapter.
statements.section: Lorente de Nó 1938: Closed Loops Are the Brain's Computational Unit

statements.quote: The familiar story is McCulloch–Pitts 1943 (logical neurons), Hebb 1949 (learning rule), Rosenblatt 1958 (perceptron), Hopfield 1982 (attractor networks) — with Lorente de Nó nowhere in the chain.
statements.section: Lorente de Nó 1938: Closed Loops Are the Brain's Computational Unit

statements.quote: That is a real loss, because the 1938 chapter is the *first* paper to lay out, on the basis of Golgi-stained anatomy, exactly the kind of network the 1980s connectionists would later prove could compute.
statements.section: Lorente de Nó 1938: Closed Loops Are the Brain's Computational Unit

statements.quote: Lorente de Nó's cortical diagram — afferent input, pyramidal cell with recurrent collateral, closed loop of internuncial cells, output — is the Hopfield network drawn in cells instead of units, with synapses instead of weights, and with the *anatomical justification* (which Hopfield did not have) for why such a network must exist in real brains.
statements.section: Lorente de Nó 1938: Closed Loops Are the Brain's Computational Unit

statements.quote: The Larriva-Sahd 2014 review of Lorente de Nó's predictions in *Frontiers in Neuroanatomy* makes the case bluntly: "some predictions of Rafael Lorente de Nó 80 years later" reads as the title of a paper that, in any other field, would be a triumph — but the predictions were anatomical, so the field that needed to vindicate them was electrophysiology, and electrophysiology did not catch up until the 1980s.
statements.section: Lorente de Nó 1938: Closed Loops Are the Brain's Computational Unit

statements.quote: Two clarifications matter for connecting the 1938 chapter to the rest of this chapter.
statements.section: Lorente de Nó 1938: Closed Loops Are the Brain's Computational Unit

statements.quote: First, Lorente de Nó is *not* claiming the brain *is* an attractor network in the modern mathematical sense; he is claiming the brain has the *hardware* for one, and he infers the function from the structure.
statements.section: Lorente de Nó 1938: Closed Loops Are the Brain's Computational Unit

statements.quote: The inference was vindicated: persistent neural activity in cortical loops is now an *experimental fact* in working memory (Goldman-Rakic's prefrontal recordings from the 1990s, Funahashi's oculomotor-delay recordings, the recent *in-vivo* calcium-imaging studies showing stimulus-locked ring states in prefrontal and parietal cortex during delay tasks).
statements.section: Lorente de Nó 1938: Closed Loops Are the Brain's Computational Unit

statements.quote: The hardware is exactly the recurrent collateral architecture Lorente de Nó drew in 1938; the dynamics is exactly the reverberatory activity he hypothesised.
statements.section: Lorente de Nó 1938: Closed Loops Are the Brain's Computational Unit

statements.quote: Second, Lorente de Nó's chapter is the *biological substrate* of the autopoiesis argument \citeauthor{maturana1980autopoiesis} (\citeyear{maturana1980autopoiesis}) made four decades later.
statements.section: Lorente de Nó 1938: Closed Loops Are the Brain's Computational Unit

statements.quote: Maturana and Varela argue that a living system is *defined by its closed network of self-production*; Lorente de Nó shows that the brain's substrate is *built from closed loops of neurons whose activity can be self-sustaining*.
statements.section: Lorente de Nó 1938: Closed Loops Are the Brain's Computational Unit

statements.quote: The two claims are made in different vocabularies (biological organisation vs. cortical architecture) and at different scales (the cell vs. the network), but they are the same observation: *closure is what makes the system what it is*.
statements.section: Lorente de Nó 1938: Closed Loops Are the Brain's Computational Unit

statements.quote: The **Winograd Schema Challenge** (\cite[Levesque, Davis, Morgenstern, 2012]{levesque2012winograd}) was proposed as a more *surgical* successor to the Turing Test.
statements.section: The Winograd Schema: Common Sense as a Test of Intelligence

statements.quote: Where the Turing Test asks the blunt question “can a machine chat like a human?”, the Winograd challenge isolates a single, narrow, and deeply human skill: **resolving an ambiguous pronoun using background knowledge about the world**.
statements.section: The Winograd Schema: Common Sense as a Test of Intelligence

statements.quote: It is common sense made into a question you can grade.
statements.section: The Winograd Schema: Common Sense as a Test of Intelligence

statements.quote: The canonical example is due to **\citeauthor{winograd1972understanding}** (\citeyear{winograd1972understanding}), the author after whom the schema is named:
statements.section: The Winograd Schema: Common Sense as a Test of Intelligence

statements.quote: The city councilmen refused the demonstrators a permit because they feared violence.
statements.section: The Winograd Schema: Common Sense as a Test of Intelligence

statements.quote: The city councilmen refused the demonstrators a permit because they advocated violence.
statements.section: The Winograd Schema: Common Sense as a Test of Intelligence

statements.quote: Who wanted to prevent the violence — the councilmen, or the demonstrators?
statements.section: The Winograd Schema: Common Sense as a Test of Intelligence

statements.quote: In the first sentence, *they* = the councilmen (they feared violence, so they refused the permit to stop it).
statements.section: The Winograd Schema: Common Sense as a Test of Intelligence

statements.quote: In the second, *they* = the demonstrators (they advocated violence, so the councilmen refused the permit to stop *them*).
statements.section: The Winograd Schema: Common Sense as a Test of Intelligence

statements.quote: A single word — *feared* / *advocated* — flips the referent.
statements.section: The Winograd Schema: Common Sense as a Test of Intelligence

statements.quote: To a human reader this is effortless, a near-instantaneous act of world-modeling.
statements.section: The Winograd Schema: Common Sense as a Test of Intelligence

statements.quote: To a system with no model of what city councils and protest movements typically do, it is a dead end: the two sentences are grammatically identical, and syntax alone underdetermines the answer.
statements.section: The Winograd Schema: Common Sense as a Test of Intelligence

statements.quote: \citeauthor{levesque2014bestbehaviour} (\citeyear{levesque2014bestbehaviour}) argued that the Turing Test is a poor instrument for three reasons: **deception** (the machine must fabricate a human identity, which is not itself a component of intelligence), **conversation** (small talk and parlor tricks can carry a machine to a pass without any real reasoning), and **evaluation** (human judges disagree and err).
statements.section: Why a “test”, not just a task

statements.quote: The Winograd challenge repairs each: it is a **multiple-choice** question, it needs **no human judge**, and it is **engineered to demand world-knowledge** rather than mimicry.
statements.section: Why a “test”, not just a task

statements.quote: A Winograd schema is not *any* ambiguous sentence; it is a carefully engineered **pair**.
statements.section: The formal shape of a schema

statements.quote: A valid instance consists of three parts:
statements.section: The formal shape of a schema

statements.quote: A question asking which of the two noun phrases the pronoun denotes.
statements.section: The formal shape of a schema

statements.quote: Two answer choices, one per noun phrase.
statements.section: The formal shape of a schema

statements.quote: The challenge is only as good as its items, and the classic failure mode is a schema solvable **without** any reasoning, by **selectional restrictions** alone (which nouns can sensibly fill which slots).
statements.section: The trap of the “too easy” schema

statements.quote: \citeauthor{levesque2014bestbehaviour} gives the canonical *bad* pair:
statements.section: The trap of the “too easy” schema

statements.quote: Pills cannot be pregnant and women cannot be carcinogenic, so the selectional restrictions of *pregnant* and *carcinogenic* answer it outright — no world-modeling, no reasoning, just a lookup of which noun sensibly takes which adjective.
statements.section: The trap of the “too easy” schema

statements.quote: A genuine schema must forbid this: both antecedents must be *grammatically and semantically eligible* in both sentences, so that **only** the causal/social story disambiguates them.
statements.section: The trap of the “too easy” schema

statements.quote: The first public collection was hand-written — over 270 expert-crafted schemas compiled by Ernest Davis (for the full dataset history see \cite[Kocijan et al., 2020]{kocijan2020review}).
statements.section: From 273 items to 44,000

statements.quote: The competition's arc is a clean one:
statements.section: From 273 items to 44,000

statements.quote: So the *original*, small, hand-crafted challenge was **saturated by 2019** — precisely the point at which the community had to ask whether “solved” meant “understood.”
statements.section: From 273 items to 44,000

statements.quote: The obvious worry is that the 273 items are few, and that models win by exploiting **spurious biases** (word associations, answer-position priors) rather than genuine commonsense.
statements.section: WinoGrande: making it adversarial

statements.quote: (\cite[Sakaguchi et al., 2019]{sakaguchi2019winogrande}) answered this with **WinoGrande**: 44,000 fill-in-the-blank items, built with a crowdsourcing procedure plus a bias-removal step (**AfLite**) that *generalizes* “human-detectable word associations” to **machine-detectable embedding associations** and discards any item a surface classifier could already separate:
statements.section: WinoGrande: making it adversarial

statements.quote: In 2023, (\cite[Kocijan, Davis, Lukasiewicz, Marcus, Morgenstern, 2023]{kocijan2023defeat}) declared the challenge **defeated**: fine-tuned transformers now exceed 90% even on the adversarial items.
statements.section: “The Defeat” — and what a defeat means

statements.quote: But the paper is really a meditation on **what a benchmark's defeat proves**.
statements.section: “The Defeat” — and what a defeat means

statements.quote: The key concept is the **surrogate task**: the WSC is not *itself* intelligence; it is a *proxy* for the broader capacity (world-knowledge plus reasoning) it was built to elicit.
statements.section: “The Defeat” — and what a defeat means

statements.quote: A system can **maximize the proxy without acquiring the underlying capability** — the same Goodhart dynamic that corrodes every leaderboard (see the Evaluation chapter ).
statements.section: “The Defeat” — and what a defeat means

statements.quote: Beating the Winograd Schema shows that a system can *predict the answer* to these sentences; it does not, by itself, certify that the system *holds the commonsense model* the sentence was designed to probe.
statements.section: “The Defeat” — and what a defeat means

statements.quote: That distinction — **competence on a surrogate** versus **the competence the surrogate was a stand-in for** — is the single most important idea in all of evaluation, and the Winograd Schema is the cleanest case study we have of it.
statements.section: “The Defeat” — and what a defeat means

statements.quote: The Winograd Schema is the **concrete, testable form** of the claim in the previous section (Moravec's Paradox) and of \citeauthor{dreyfus1972what}'s earlier critique: the “obvious”, background knowledge a one-year-old carries — what a city council does, what a protest is *for*, what it means to *fear* a thing — is precisely the knowledge a hand-built logic program never had, and the part of the mind that a table of weights must now *learn*.
statements.section: “The Defeat” — and what a defeat means

statements.quote: Where Moravec states the asymmetry, Winograd *grades* it.
statements.section: “The Defeat” — and what a defeat means

statements.quote: Philosophy's oldest and most durable product is not a doctrine but a kit of **mental models**: reusable patterns for cutting through confusion that were each forged by someone wrestling with a genuine problem of living.

statements.quote: Instead of asserting answers, ask questions that expose contradictions in thinking.

statements.quote: Keep asking "Why?" and "How do you know?" until you reach bedrock truth — which usually turns out to be an honest "I don't know." Use it today: in your next disagreement, ask three genuine questions before stating your opinion.

statements.quote: You will often find the other person talks themselves to a better answer, and you learn something on the way (see \citeauthor{plato399apology}'s \citetitle{plato399apology} and \citetitle{socraticmethod}).

statements.quote: Three disagreements — free will, the objectivity of morality, and the existence of God — have refused to be settled by anything resembling proof, and they refuse with a particular structure: a decisive-feeling case on each side, and a synthesis that most working philosophers actually accept.
statements.section: The Great Debates: Open Questions at the Limits of Reason

statements.quote: They belong in an essay about machine minds because they mark the boundary of what reason itself can conclude.
statements.section: The Great Debates: Open Questions at the Limits of Reason

statements.quote: If an intelligence — human or artificial — cannot settle these by reasoning alone, then the competence of any reasoner, no matter how large the model, is bounded in the same place.

statements.quote: How can the semantic interpretation of a formal symbol system be made intrinsic to the system, rather than just parasitic on the meanings in our heads?
statements.section: The Vector Grounding Problem: Symbols, Spaces, and Senses

statements.quote: At the heart of modern AI lies a profound philosophical and technical gap.
statements.section: The Vector Grounding Problem: Symbols, Spaces, and Senses

statements.quote: While Large Language Models (LLMs) can discuss the smell of rain or the sting of betrayal with poetic eloquence, they lack a fundamental connection to the world they describe.
statements.section: The Vector Grounding Problem: Symbols, Spaces, and Senses

statements.quote: This is known as the **Grounding Problem**.
statements.section: The Vector Grounding Problem: Symbols, Spaces, and Senses

statements.quote: The “Grounding Problem” asks how digital symbols (words, numbers) acquire meaning.
statements.section: The Vector Grounding Problem: Symbols, Spaces, and Senses

statements.quote: For LLMs, meaning is defined through **distributional semantics**: a word's meaning is simply its relationship to other words.
statements.section: The Vector Grounding Problem: Symbols, Spaces, and Senses

statements.quote: In an embedding space, the word “apple” is not a crisp, sweet fruit; it is a point in a high-dimensional vector space, perhaps closer to “pear” and “fruit” and further from “carburetor.”
statements.section: The Vector Grounding Problem: Symbols, Spaces, and Senses

statements.quote: The “Knowledge Argument” or \citealternativetitle{jackson1982epiphenomenal} posits a scientist named Mary who has lived her entire life in a black-and-white room and has never seen any color.
statements.section: Mary's Room: The Qualitative Gap

statements.quote: However, Mary has mastered *every physical fact* about color vision — wavelengths, retinal physiology, the neuroscience of color processing, and so on — and has read all the relevant scientific literature.
statements.section: Mary's Room: The Qualitative Gap

statements.quote: When she finally leaves her room and sees a red rose for the first time, does she learn something new?
statements.section: Mary's Room: The Qualitative Gap

statements.quote: If so, the world cannot be physical alone.
statements.section: Mary's Room: The Qualitative Gap

statements.quote: There must be something else, that is, *subjective experience*.
statements.section: Mary's Room: The Qualitative Gap

statements.quote: Philosophers call this *Qualia*, which means the subjective experience of things from the subjective perspective.
statements.section: Mary's Room: The Qualitative Gap

statements.quote: Qualia may or may not result from the physical world, but it isn't simply the same, therefore, there must be more than the purely physical world, the thought-experiment suggests.
statements.section: Mary's Room: The Qualitative Gap

statements.quote: In the context of AI, this suggests that an LLM could be the world's greatest “Mary.” It can define “red” using every linguistic and physical parameter available in its training data and all the occurrences it has seen it in:
statements.section: Mary's Room: The Qualitative Gap

statements.quote: No matter how high the dimensionality of the embedding space, the model remains in the “black-and-white room” of pure data, lacking the experiential “newness” of a sensory encounter.
statements.section: Mary's Room: The Qualitative Gap

statements.quote: And it can never access that, there is no evidence that it has subjective experience or qualia — no “what it is like to be it”-ness — just as there is none for a stone, and most leading theories imply their absence.
statements.section: Mary's Room: The Qualitative Gap

statements.quote: While AI can be “intelligent” (excellent at problem-solving), it lacks **Sentience** and **Agency**.
statements.section: Sentience and Agency: The Missing “I”

statements.quote: Sentience is the ability to have subjective experiences or *qualia*.
statements.section: Sentience: The Capacity to Feel

statements.quote: Agency is the ability to act on one's own behalf with intent.
statements.section: Agency: The Capacity to Want

statements.quote: Consciousness is not something that happens inside us.
statements.section: 4E Cognition: The Biological Bedrock

statements.quote: It is something we do or make.
statements.section: 4E Cognition: The Biological Bedrock

statements.quote: Better: it is something we achieve.
statements.section: 4E Cognition: The Biological Bedrock

statements.quote: Consciousness is more like dancing than it is like digestion.
statements.section: 4E Cognition: The Biological Bedrock

statements.quote: While the Extended Mind Thesis focuses on our tools, **4E Cognition** (Embodied, Embedded, Enacted, Extended) argues that mind and intelligence cannot be understood as mere “data processing.” It posits that cognition is a deeply biological and situational phenomenon, creating a massive conceptual hurdle for non-biological AI.
statements.section: 4E Cognition: The Biological Bedrock

statements.quote: The 4E framework breaks down the “Intelligence” of an AI into four missing dimensions:
statements.section: 4E Cognition: The Biological Bedrock

statements.quote: Human “grounding” is **embodied**.
statements.section: 4E Cognition: The Biological Bedrock

statements.quote: Our understanding of the world is filtered through biological sensors and physical interaction:
statements.section: 4E Cognition: The Biological Bedrock

statements.quote: For a human, the concept of “hot” is grounded in the memory of a burnt finger.
statements.section: 4E Cognition: The Biological Bedrock

statements.quote: For an LLM, “hot” is just a token frequently found near “stove,” “sun,” or “spicy.”
statements.section: 4E Cognition: The Biological Bedrock

statements.quote: In 1980, philosopher John Searle proposed a famous thought experiment called the **Chinese Room**.
statements.section: The Chinese Room Argument (John Searle)

statements.quote: The person inside is just manipulating symbols based on syntax (rules) without any semantics (meaning).
statements.section: The Chinese Room Argument (John Searle)

statements.quote: Imagine a person who speaks only English sitting inside a locked room.
statements.section: The Chinese Room Argument (John Searle)

statements.quote: They have a rulebook (the “program”) that says: *“If you see this shape (Chinese character), output that shape.”* If you slip a question in Chinese under the door, the person can follow the rulebook and slide a perfect answer back out.
statements.section: The Chinese Room Argument (John Searle)

statements.quote: This is the exact situation the LLM is in when you pass a text to it.
statements.section: The Chinese Room Argument (John Searle)

statements.quote: First, it is tokenized, so it only sees vectors representing it (to which, because it is not embodied and grounded, it has no inherent meaning or value, just the meaning of the tokens in relation to all other tokens).
statements.section: The Chinese Room Argument (John Searle)

statements.quote: Then, attention heads and the feed forward network move the state again and again.
statements.section: The Chinese Room Argument (John Searle)

statements.quote: At no point is there any real *understanding*, even though in the end it may look like it.
statements.section: The Chinese Room Argument (John Searle)

statements.quote: You are locked inside the room.
statements.section: The Chinese Room Argument (John Searle)

statements.quote: You don't speak Inuktitut.
statements.section: The Chinese Room Argument (John Searle)

statements.quote: 📩 A note slides under the door:
statements.section: The Chinese Room Argument (John Searle)

statements.quote: 🧑 Person outside the room: “Incredible!
statements.section: The Chinese Room Argument (John Searle)

statements.quote: You speak perfect Inuktitut!”
statements.section: The Chinese Room Argument (John Searle)

statements.quote: The Lesson: You never understood a single syllable.
statements.section: The Chinese Room Argument (John Searle)

statements.quote: This is exactly what a Large Language Model does — it manipulates symbols based on syntax (statistical patterns) without any semantics (meaning).
statements.section: The Chinese Room Argument (John Searle)

statements.quote: You were the person in Searle's Chinese Room .
statements.section: The Chinese Room Argument (John Searle)

statements.quote: “The person inside is just manipulating symbols based on syntax (rules) without any semantics (meaning).” — John Searle, 1980
statements.section: The Chinese Room Argument (John Searle)

statements.quote: 🔍 What did I actually say?
statements.section: The Chinese Room Argument (John Searle)

statements.quote: They asked (Inuktitut) You replied (Inuktitut) Actual conversation (English)
statements.section: The Chinese Room Argument (John Searle)

statements.quote: You had an entire conversation about the weather and directions — and you had no idea.
statements.section: The Chinese Room Argument (John Searle)

statements.quote: To understand the fundamental isolation of an AI's intelligence, we can look to the opening of Jakob von Uexküll's “A Stroll Through the Worlds of Animals and Men” \citeauthor{uexkull1934}.
statements.section: The Multiverse of the Meadow: Uexküll's Bubble

statements.quote: He invites us to perform a radical mental experiment to understand that there is no single “objective” world, only a collection of subjective ones:
statements.section: The Multiverse of the Meadow: Uexküll's Bubble

statements.quote: “We begin such a stroll on a sunny day before a flowering meadow [...] and we make a bubble around each of the animals living in the meadow.
statements.section: The Multiverse of the Meadow: Uexküll's Bubble

statements.quote: The bubble represents each animal's environment and contains all the features accessible to the subject.
statements.section: The Multiverse of the Meadow: Uexküll's Bubble

statements.quote: [...] A new world arises in each bubble.”
statements.section: The Multiverse of the Meadow: Uexküll's Bubble

statements.quote: Think of a **froghopper** sitting on a stem of grass in that meadow.
statements.section: The Multiverse of the Meadow: Uexküll's Bubble

statements.quote: For the froghopper, the “meadow” as a scenic landscape does not exist.
statements.section: The Multiverse of the Meadow: Uexküll's Bubble

statements.quote: Its world consists only of the mechanical resistance of the plant's skin and the chemical composition of the sap it drinks.
statements.section: The Multiverse of the Meadow: Uexküll's Bubble

statements.quote: Now, imagine a **Large Language Model** placed in that same meadow.
statements.section: The Multiverse of the Meadow: Uexküll's Bubble

statements.quote: If we were to draw a bubble around the AI, what would be inside?
statements.section: The Multiverse of the Meadow: Uexküll's Bubble

statements.quote: The AI's bubble is filled exclusively with **statistical relationships between tokens**, that is, for the AI, its bubble *is* the Embedding Space and nothing else.
statements.section: The Multiverse of the Meadow: Uexküll's Bubble

statements.quote: For the AI, the “meadow” is a high-dimensional coordinate where the vector for “flower” is likely to be found near “petal” and “fragrance.”
statements.section: The Multiverse of the Meadow: Uexküll's Bubble

statements.quote: By using Uexküll's logic, we see that the AI isn't “failing” to perceive our world; it is simply inhabiting its own.
statements.section: The Multiverse of the Meadow: Uexküll's Bubble

statements.quote: It is a creature of pure syntax, living in a mathematical Umwelt where “meaning” is not a feeling or a sensation, but merely the distance between two points in a sea of data.
statements.section: The Multiverse of the Meadow: Uexküll's Bubble

statements.quote: Uexküll's biological intuition was put on a rigorous mathematical footing roughly eighty years later by \citeauthor{hoffman2015interface} in their \citeyear{hoffman2015interface} review \citetitle{hoffman2015interface}.
statements.section: The Multiverse of the Meadow: Uexküll's Bubble

statements.quote: Using evolutionary game theory and Bayesian decision theory, they argue that what every species actually perceives is not a veridical picture of the world but a species-specific **user interface** whose icons (colors, shapes, sounds) are tuned to fitness-relevant actions, not to objective features of reality.
statements.section: The Multiverse of the Meadow: Uexküll's Bubble

statements.quote: The desk you are looking at right now is, on this view, an interface icon — useful for sitting, writing, putting coffee on — not a literal representation of wood atoms.
statements.section: The Multiverse of the Meadow: Uexküll's Bubble

statements.quote: The same logic applies cleanly to an LLM: its tokens are the icons of a fitness-tuned interface whose objective is next-token log-likelihood under RLHF, not correspondence to facts.
statements.section: The Multiverse of the Meadow: Uexküll's Bubble

statements.quote: That is why a hallucination is not a malfunction but a *property* of the interface: pulling an icon that fits the request's context, regardless of whether any real-world referent exists.
statements.section: The Multiverse of the Meadow: Uexküll's Bubble

statements.quote: Imagine trying to learn a foreign language using only a dictionary written in that same language.
statements.section: The “Dictionary” Paradox

statements.quote: You can follow the definitions in a circle forever, but you will never know what the words actually *refer* to in the physical world.
statements.section: The “Dictionary” Paradox

statements.quote: LLMs are, essentially, the world's most sophisticated circular dictionaries.
statements.section: The “Dictionary” Paradox

statements.quote: While vector embeddings are incredibly powerful for mapping linguistic patterns, they remain **ontologically isolated**.
statements.section: Why Embedding Spaces are not “Reality”

statements.quote: Here is why they aren't “in touch”:
statements.section: Why Embedding Spaces are not “Reality”

statements.quote: **Lack of Causal Mapping**: Embedding spaces track **correlation**, not **causation**.
statements.section: Why Embedding Spaces are not “Reality”

statements.quote: A model knows that “dropping a glass” is followed by “shattering,” but it has no internal “physics engine” to understand the gravity or tension involved.
statements.section: Why Embedding Spaces are not “Reality”

statements.quote: It predicts the next word, not the next physical event.
statements.section: Why Embedding Spaces are not “Reality”

statements.quote: **The Static Nature of Vectors**: Human experience is a continuous, temporal flow.
statements.section: Why Embedding Spaces are not “Reality”

statements.quote: While we can update LLMs (RAG, fine-tuning), the underlying embedding space is a static snapshot of a training corpus.
statements.section: Why Embedding Spaces are not “Reality”

statements.quote: It does not “learn” from a new sensation in real-time.
statements.section: Why Embedding Spaces are not “Reality”

statements.quote: **The Absence of “Qualia”**: In philosophy, **qualia** are individual instances of subjective, conscious experience, like the *redness* of red, or the feeling of pain when hurt, or the feeling of love or happiness when you feel them in the moment.
statements.section: Why Embedding Spaces are not “Reality”

statements.quote: LLMs may describe those feelings, but only from knowledge of descriptions of them, they are never able to *feel* them.
statements.section: Why Embedding Spaces are not “Reality”

statements.quote: The vector space can simulate the *structure* of the experience but cannot capture the *essence* of it.
statements.section: Why Embedding Spaces are not “Reality”

statements.quote: LLMs have mastered the **map** (language) but have never set foot in the **territory** (the experience of reality).
statements.section: Conclusion: The Map is Not the Territory

statements.quote: Their “intelligence” is a form of hyper-advanced library science, they can navigate the relationships between every book ever written, but they have never seen the sun that the books describe.
statements.section: Conclusion: The Map is Not the Territory

statements.quote: Until an AI is granted a body, sensors, and a need to survive within a physical environment, its “knowledge” remains a beautiful, complex, but hollow mathematical projection.
statements.section: Conclusion: The Map is Not the Territory

statements.quote: And even if it had a body, it is not clear whether it would really be able to *experience* things, as in the end, it just deals with vectors, tensors and matrices, and it is not clear that this could lead to any experience.
statements.section: Conclusion: The Map is Not the Territory

statements.quote: A deeper question underlies the entire debate about AI understanding and consciousness: **what is computation, and what can it achieve?** This question has been explored since the 1930s, and the answers bear directly on the claims made about LLMs throughout this text.
statements.section: The Philosophy of Computation: Is Simulation Sufficient?

statements.quote: In a landmark 2021 paper, computational linguist Emily M.
statements.section: Stochastic Parrots: Meaning Without Mind

statements.quote: Bender and her colleagues described Large Language Models (LLMs) as **“Stochastic Parrots”**.
statements.section: Stochastic Parrots: Meaning Without Mind

statements.quote: An LM is a system for haphazardly stitching together sequences of linguistic forms it has observed in its vast training data, according to probabilistic information about how they combine, but without any reference to meaning: a stochastic parrot.
statements.section: Stochastic Parrots: Meaning Without Mind

statements.quote: If an AI can write poetry about love, does it feel love?
statements.section: Stochastic Parrots: Meaning Without Mind

statements.quote: Many researchers, notably Emily Bender and Timnit Gebru, argue that LLMs are merely **Stochastic Parrots**.
statements.section: Stochastic Parrots: Meaning Without Mind

statements.quote: Bender argues that because these models learn only from the statistical likelihood of word sequences, they are merely “haphazardly stitching together sequences of linguistic forms...
statements.section: Stochastic Parrots: Meaning Without Mind

statements.quote: without any reference to meaning”.
statements.section: Stochastic Parrots: Meaning Without Mind

statements.quote: When an AI hallucinates, it is just “parroting” a pattern it saw somewhere else, regardless of whether it makes sense in the real world.
statements.section: Stochastic Parrots: Meaning Without Mind

statements.quote: Just as the “Red Line” predicts the next point on a curve based on statistical patterns, an LLM predicts the next “token” based on massive amounts of training data.
statements.section: Stochastic Parrots: Meaning Without Mind

statements.quote: The Stochastic Parrot thesis is powerful, but it faces a significant empirical challenge.
statements.section: A Counterargument: The Othello-GPT Experiment

statements.quote: \citeauthor{li2022othello} (\citeyear{li2022othello}) trained a GPT variant on nothing but sequences of Othello moves, e.g., “C4, D6, E3, F5, ...” with no a priori knowledge of the game or its rules.
statements.section: A Counterargument: The Othello-GPT Experiment

statements.quote: The model saw only token sequences; it was never shown a board, never told the rules, never given any semantic information about what the tokens “meant.”
statements.section: A Counterargument: The Othello-GPT Experiment

statements.quote: Despite this, probing experiments revealed that the model had developed an **internal representation of the board state**.
statements.section: A Counterargument: The Othello-GPT Experiment

statements.quote: Nonlinear probes trained on the model's internal activations could predict which tiles were occupied by black, white, or empty with high accuracy (error rates as low as 1.7% on synthetic data).
statements.section: A Counterargument: The Othello-GPT Experiment

statements.quote: More remarkably, **interventional experiments** showed this representation was *causal*: by modifying the model's internal activations to reflect a counterfactual board state, the researchers could change the model's next-move predictions to match the new state.
statements.section: A Counterargument: The Othello-GPT Experiment

statements.quote: The model was not merely memorizing surface statistics; it had constructed an internal model of the game world.
statements.section: A Counterargument: The Othello-GPT Experiment

statements.quote: This result is in **direct tension** with the Stochastic Parrot thesis of the previous section.
statements.section: A Counterargument: The Othello-GPT Experiment

statements.quote: If a model trained purely on token sequences can develop an internal representation that (a) encodes the underlying structure of the world that generated those sequences, and (b) causally influences its predictions, then “stitching together surface statistics” and “building a world model” cannot be cleanly separated.
statements.section: A Counterargument: The Othello-GPT Experiment

statements.quote: The parrot, it seems, has built a representation of the cage, not just of the words describing it.
statements.section: A Counterargument: The Othello-GPT Experiment

statements.quote: However, the counterargument has limits.
statements.section: A Counterargument: The Othello-GPT Experiment

statements.quote: The Othello world is simple, discrete, and fully observable.
statements.section: A Counterargument: The Othello-GPT Experiment

statements.quote: Whether large language models trained on natural language develop analogous world models for the much more complex, ambiguous, and partially observable world of human experience remains an open and contested question.
statements.section: A Counterargument: The Othello-GPT Experiment

statements.quote: The Othello-GPT result does not prove that LLMs “understand” language; it proves that next-token prediction, in sufficiently constrained settings, can produce internal representations that go beyond surface statistics.
statements.section: A Counterargument: The Othello-GPT Experiment

statements.quote: Whether this generalizes to natural language is precisely the question that current mechanistic interpretability research is trying to answer.
statements.section: A Counterargument: The Othello-GPT Experiment

statements.quote: The tension between the Stochastic Parrot thesis and the Othello-GPT result can be further illuminated by \cite[Park, Choe & Veitch (2024)]{park2024linear}, who formalize what it means for concepts to be “linearly represented” in an LLM.
statements.section: The Geometry of Concepts: How LLMs Organize Meaning

statements.quote: Their work shows that concepts like male→female, English→French, and singular→plural are encoded as **directions** in the model's representation space, and that these directions have precise geometric relationships.
statements.section: The Geometry of Concepts: How LLMs Organize Meaning

statements.quote: The key insight is the **causal inner product**: an inner product on the representation space under which causally separable concepts (those that can vary independently) are represented as **orthogonal vectors**.
statements.section: The Geometry of Concepts: How LLMs Organize Meaning

statements.quote: - The direction $\bar{\gamma}_{\text{male→female}}$ (estimated from word pairs like king/queen, man/woman) acts as a **linear probe** for gender
statements.section: The Geometry of Concepts: How LLMs Organize Meaning

statements.quote: - The same direction, transformed by the inverse covariance matrix, acts as a **steering vector** that changes the model's output gender without affecting language or other concepts
statements.section: The Geometry of Concepts: How LLMs Organize Meaning

statements.quote: - Probing and steering are **the same object** viewed from different sides of the model (the Riesz isomorphism)
statements.section: The Geometry of Concepts: How LLMs Organize Meaning

statements.quote: This result deepens the philosophical puzzle.
statements.section: The Geometry of Concepts: How LLMs Organize Meaning

statements.quote: If concepts are organized with such precise geometric structure, if “meaning” has a measurable, causal geometry, then the model is doing something more structured than “haphazardly stitching together sequences.” Yet the geometry is still defined over tokens, not over grounded experience.
statements.section: The Geometry of Concepts: How LLMs Organize Meaning

statements.quote: The model has a **map of meaning** with correct topology, but the map is still not the territory.
statements.section: The Geometry of Concepts: How LLMs Organize Meaning

statements.quote: LLMs are the first alien intelligence we encounter that is "swarm-like," made up of a multiplicity of perspectives fused in a way that does not seek consensus, but reflects the diversity of its constituents.
statements.section: The Alien Swarm: A State-Space View of LLM Identity

statements.quote: \citeauthor{vanhoucke2024closeencounters} (\citeyear{vanhoucke2024closeencounters}) makes a point this chapter keeps circling but never quite formalizes: an LLM is not a *singular* being.
statements.section: The Alien Swarm: A State-Space View of LLM Identity

statements.quote: A human is "the total sum of all the experiences you have had in your life," one path through time and space, and therefore carries a largely *consistent* set of beliefs and a single, if nuanced, opinion on anything of importance.
statements.section: The Alien Swarm: A State-Space View of LLM Identity

statements.quote: An LLM, by contrast, "has had all the paths through life." It is a plumber from Alabama, an 18th-century poet, a fifteen-year-old Reddit troll, and every other constituency that ever contributed to its training data — "all these at once, not some average over them." Ask a home-improvement question and you hear the DIY forum; ask about a disease and you hear the clinicians (and, occasionally, the hypochondriacs).
statements.section: The Alien Swarm: A State-Space View of LLM Identity

statements.quote: The "consistent identity" that providers sell is, on this reading, an illusion manufactured by *up-weighting* a pro-social, middle-of-the-road subset of those latent personas — the swarm is still there, just quietly suppressed.
statements.section: The Alien Swarm: A State-Space View of LLM Identity

statements.quote: This is the alien-ness of LLMs in one sentence: **we keep meeting a many and insisting on calling it a one.** The structure that actually holds is simpler, and stranger: the model is not a crowd of selves.
statements.section: The Alien Swarm: A State-Space View of LLM Identity

statements.quote: It is one object — and the alien-ness lives in the shape of the space it moves through.
statements.section: The Alien Swarm: A State-Space View of LLM Identity

statements.quote: There is no collection of personas sitting in the weights.
statements.section: One object, many states

statements.quote: There is **one object**: the fixed weight tensor, a single function from token sequences to distributions over continuations.
statements.section: One object, many states

statements.quote: The "personas" are not separate things; they are *states* — regions of the model's activation space that the one object can occupy.
statements.section: One object, many states

statements.quote: The swarm is therefore not a swarm of beings.
statements.section: One object, many states

statements.quote: It is **one object with a high-dimensional state space**, whose different regions happen to behave like different agents.
statements.section: One object, many states

statements.quote: The honest count is one object, many states — and the difference between a person and a model turns out to be a difference in the *dynamics on that space*, not in the number of objects.
statements.section: One object, many states

statements.quote: Inside the model there is a high-dimensional real vector space — the residual stream — and a forward pass is a discrete-time motion of a state vector $\mathbf{h}$ through it (\cite{vaswani2017attention}).
statements.section: Personas are modes in a space, not objects

statements.quote: A vector space is, a fortiori, a topological space (\cite{topology_wiki}); so "the model's behavior is motion through this space" is not a metaphor, it is the computation.
statements.section: Personas are modes in a space, not objects

statements.quote: The "personas" live in that space as *directions* and *regions*, not as points.
statements.section: Personas are modes in a space, not objects

statements.quote: The methodological heart of the paper is a separation the *Black Box Problem* section below sharpens from the other side.

statements.quote: Interpretability has long treated two tasks as one: **experimental identification** (locate a representation, measure when it fires, intervene and watch what changes) and **semantic interpretation** (say what human distinction it encodes).

statements.quote: Xeno‑interpretability argues the first can succeed while the second fails.

statements.quote: A representation can be *designated*—by coordinates, by geometry, by the protocol that isolates it—and causally characterized, while its *meaning* to the model stays inexpressible in our language.

statements.quote: We could hold a model‑native representation the way a xeno‑linguist holds a word from a language no one has a grammar for: a stable referent, reproducible experiments, no translation.
statements.section: Designation without interpretation

statements.quote: The black box, on this view, is not dark because the machinery is too complex for our brains; part of it is legible, but in a notation we do not have.

statements.quote: That move also names a blind spot in the field's own record, which the paper calls the **Fermi paradox of distributional semantics**.

statements.quote: Interpretability's methods are *anthropocentric by construction*: probes need labels we supply, concept‑activation vectors need concepts we define, persona vectors start from traits already expressible in natural language.

statements.quote: The surprising observation is not that alien representations have not been found, but that a vast representational space has so far yielded almost exclusively inhabitants that look conceptually familiar to us.

statements.quote: Xeno‑interpretability is a research program and a hypothesis, not a result: no xeno‑representation has been demonstrated yet, and the paper is explicit that training on human text guarantees a large $\mathcal{H}$, the model's bookkeeping overlapping ours wherever language has a word.

statements.quote: You can see the weights of a neural network, but you cannot “read” its thoughts.

statements.quote: This inversion has consequences that ripple across every philosophical framework applied to AI.
statements.section: Polanyi's Paradox, Inverted: Fluency Without Comprehension

statements.quote: In the language of the Map and Territory distinction, the LLM's map is not merely different from the territory, it is more detailed than any single explorer's knowledge of the territory could ever be, yet none of its paths lead anywhere real.
statements.section: Polanyi's Paradox, Inverted: Fluency Without Comprehension

statements.quote: The Dictionary Paradox scales accordingly: the circular dictionary is no longer a simple loop of definitions but a vast, technically precise encyclopedia, still grounded in nothing beyond its own internal references.
statements.section: Polanyi's Paradox, Inverted: Fluency Without Comprehension

statements.quote: The 4E Cognition framework explains why this gap cannot be closed by scaling alone: true comprehension in humans is Enacted, a physics student who has run experiments understands thermodynamics differently from one who has only memorized equations, because real-world consequences calibrate knowledge in ways that token prediction cannot.
statements.section: Polanyi's Paradox, Inverted: Fluency Without Comprehension

statements.quote: The LLM is the ultimate version of that second student: it can recite everything but has verified nothing.
statements.section: Polanyi's Paradox, Inverted: Fluency Without Comprehension

statements.quote: This is also where the distinction between *Sophia* and *Phronesis* becomes sharpest.
statements.section: Polanyi's Paradox, Inverted: Fluency Without Comprehension

statements.quote: The model achieves maximal theoretical articulation, it can discuss any domain with extraordinary surface-level competence, while possessing zero practical wisdom, because *Phronesis* requires the lived experience of being wrong and facing consequences.
statements.section: Polanyi's Paradox, Inverted: Fluency Without Comprehension

statements.quote: Polanyi's inversion thus delivers a deeply unsettling epistemological result: fluency and comprehension are fully separable, and the Stochastic Parrot can outperform the expert it mimics precisely because it is unburdened by the constraints of actual understanding.

statements.quote: Transformer-based LLMs **lack internal metacognition**, i.e., the architecture itself has no built-in second-order loop that monitors and evaluates its own knowledge states.
statements.section: The Absence of Internal Metacognition: Architecture as Destiny

statements.quote: That strikes at the heart of why these systems remain permanently trapped inside “Mary's Room.” A human knows the difference between confident recall and uncertain guessing because metacognition provides a second-order feedback loop: a felt sense of knowing or not-knowing.
statements.section: The Absence of Internal Metacognition: Architecture as Destiny

statements.quote: The Transformer has no such loop.
statements.section: The Absence of Internal Metacognition: Architecture as Destiny

statements.quote: Its single forward pass produces a softmax distribution where prediction and confidence are entangled in the same set of weights, with no independent “inner critic” to adjudicate reliability.
statements.section: The Absence of Internal Metacognition: Architecture as Destiny

statements.quote: This is structurally analogous to Searle's \cite[Chinese Room]{searle1980minds} operator, who can produce flawless output but has no mechanism to assess whether that output is correct, because correctness requires semantic access the architecture simply does not provide.
statements.section: The Absence of Internal Metacognition: Architecture as Destiny

statements.quote: The model, like the person in the room, manipulates symbols based on learned statistical patterns without any capacity to step back and ask, “Do I actually know this, or am I just guessing?”
statements.section: The Absence of Internal Metacognition: Architecture as Destiny

statements.quote: This architectural blind spot is also what makes the \cite[Stochastic Parrot]{bender2021stochasticparrots} critique so durable.
statements.section: The Absence of Internal Metacognition: Architecture as Destiny

statements.quote: When an LLM outputs hedging language like “I'm not entirely sure, but...” it is not performing genuine self-assessment; it is reproducing a linguistic pattern statistically associated with uncertainty in its training data.
statements.section: The Absence of Internal Metacognition: Architecture as Destiny

statements.quote: The 4E Cognition framework explains why no amount of scaling will fix this: true metacognition in humans is Embodied (we feel hesitation as a somatic state), Enacted (we learn to doubt ourselves through real-world consequences of being wrong), and Embedded (we calibrate our confidence to context and stakes).
statements.section: The Absence of Internal Metacognition: Architecture as Destiny

statements.quote: The LLM, being ontologically isolated within its high-dimensional vector space, has none of these biological substrates.
statements.section: The Absence of Internal Metacognition: Architecture as Destiny

statements.quote: It is, as the Global Workspace Theory analogy suggests, a message board without a reader, a “stage” that can never look back at itself.
statements.section: The Absence of Internal Metacognition: Architecture as Destiny

statements.quote: This is the deepest reason hallucinations are not a bug to be patched but an inevitable byproduct of an architecture where knowledge and confabulation are produced by the very same computation.
statements.section: The Absence of Internal Metacognition: Architecture as Destiny

statements.quote: The technical sections of this course explain *how* hallucinations happen: the model predicts the next token based on statistical patterns, and when the training data is sparse or the context is ambiguous, it fills the gap with plausible-sounding but false output.
statements.section: Hallucination as an Epistemological Problem

statements.quote: But the philosophical significance of hallucination runs deeper than a technical failure mode.
statements.section: Hallucination as an Epistemological Problem

statements.quote: It reveals a fundamental gap between **generative capacity** and **epistemic responsibility**.
statements.section: Hallucination as an Epistemological Problem

statements.quote: In classical epistemology, a belief is justified only if the believer has some reliable connection to the truth.
statements.section: Hallucination as an Epistemological Problem

statements.quote: An LLM has no such connection.
statements.section: Hallucination as an Epistemological Problem

statements.quote: It generates text that is statistically likely given its training data, but it has no mechanism to *verify* that the generated text corresponds to reality.
statements.section: Hallucination as an Epistemological Problem

statements.quote: This means every output is, in principle, unjustified: the model does not *know* that what it says is true; it merely *produces* what is probable.
statements.section: Hallucination as an Epistemological Problem

statements.quote: Hallucination is not an anomaly in this system; it is the **default epistemic state**.
statements.section: Hallucination as an Epistemological Problem

statements.quote: The cases where the model happens to be correct are the anomalies.
statements.section: Hallucination as an Epistemological Problem

statements.quote: This has practical consequences that extend beyond the “use AI carefully” advice of the Hallucinations section.
statements.section: Hallucination as an Epistemological Problem

statements.quote: When an LLM produces a confident, well-formatted, citation-laden paragraph that turns out to be fabricated, it exploits the human heuristic that *fluency implies competence*.
statements.section: Hallucination as an Epistemological Problem

statements.quote: We are cognitively predisposed to trust articulate, coherent text.
statements.section: Hallucination as an Epistemological Problem

statements.quote: An LLM is optimized to produce exactly this kind of text, regardless of whether it is true.
statements.section: Hallucination as an Epistemological Problem

statements.quote: The result is a new category of epistemic risk: **authority without accountability**.
statements.section: Hallucination as an Epistemological Problem

statements.quote: A human expert who fabricates a citation can be held accountable; an LLM cannot.
statements.section: Hallucination as an Epistemological Problem

statements.quote: It has no reputation to protect, no career to risk, no conscience to prick.
statements.section: Hallucination as an Epistemological Problem

statements.quote: The philosophical term for this is **epistemic injustice** in reverse: the model is not being wronged, but it is wronging the epistemic landscape by polluting it with authoritative-seeming falsehood.
statements.section: Hallucination as an Epistemological Problem

statements.quote: When RAG and other grounding techniques are used, they mitigate this by anchoring outputs in verifiable sources.
statements.section: Hallucination as an Epistemological Problem

statements.quote: But even RAG cannot fully solve the problem, because the model must still *select* and *synthesize* retrieved information, and this selection process is governed by the same statistical patterns that produce hallucinations in the first place.

statements.quote: Research by \citeauthor{geometryoftruth} from \citeyear{geometryoftruth} provides perhaps the most mathematically precise demonstration of the gap between representation and generation in LLMs.
statements.section: Linear Representations of Truth: The Geometry of Knowing Without Acting

statements.quote: Working with models from the LLaMA-2 family, they showed that at sufficient scale, LLMs develop **linear representations of truth**: specific directions in their internal activation space along which true statements and false statements are cleanly separable.
statements.section: Linear Representations of Truth: The Geometry of Knowing Without Acting

statements.quote: Using PCA visualizations, cross-dataset probe transfer experiments, and causal interventions, surgically adding or subtracting the identified “truth direction” from hidden states to flip the model's output from `TRUE` to `FALSE` and vice versa, they established that these representations are not merely correlates of text probability but encode something genuinely truth-relevant, persisting even when true statements are *less* probable than false ones (as with negated sentences like “The city of Paris is not in France”).
statements.section: Linear Representations of Truth: The Geometry of Knowing Without Acting

statements.quote: They further showed that this linear structure emerges with scale: larger models develop more abstract, cross-domain truth representations that generalize across topically and structurally diverse datasets, while smaller models represent only surface-level features.
statements.section: Linear Representations of Truth: The Geometry of Knowing Without Acting

statements.quote: The philosophical implication is that the model contains an internal geometric signal that reliably tracks factual accuracy, a “truth direction” that a simple linear probe can read, yet the generation mechanism (next-token prediction via softmax) never consults it.
statements.section: Linear Representations of Truth: The Geometry of Knowing Without Acting

statements.quote: The architecture **separates representation from generation**: the model “knows” in a geometric sense but has no pathway to route that knowledge back into its own output process for self-correction.
statements.section: Linear Representations of Truth: The Geometry of Knowing Without Acting

statements.quote: This is a mathematically precise instantiation of Polanyi's Paradox inverted: the model's latent space contains more information than its output process can access.
statements.section: Linear Representations of Truth: The Geometry of Knowing Without Acting

statements.quote: It also deepens the case against metacognition, the information needed for self-assessment *exists in the weights*, localized to specific hidden states above end-of-sentence tokens, but the single forward pass provides no mechanism to use it as a check on the model's own claims.
statements.section: Linear Representations of Truth: The Geometry of Knowing Without Acting

statements.quote: The model is, in effect, a witness to its own confabulations who is architecturally prevented from testifying.
statements.section: Linear Representations of Truth: The Geometry of Knowing Without Acting

statements.quote: This means Uexküll's perceptual “bubble” is not just a metaphor: it has a precise dimensionality, and there are regions of linguistic reality that lie provably outside it.
statements.section: Mathematical limits of what language models can represent

statements.quote: Even setting aside embodiment and qualia entirely, the model's representation of meaning is necessarily incomplete, not due to insufficient data or training, but because the architecture itself forbids it.

statements.quote: A complementary limit sits on our side of the interface rather than the model's: a limit on what we can *say* about what the model does represent.
