statements.quote: \cite[Pierucci et al. (2026)]{pierucci2026xenointerpretability} note that the model's internal state space admits a powerset-sized zoo of possible distinctions, while the properties nameable by *finite* descriptions—everything a scientist can ever write down in words, formulas, or code—are at most countable.

statements.quote: The space of what the model *could* distinguish therefore outruns the space of what we *could* name, and the gap is structural, not a failure of effort.

statements.quote: Long before artificial intelligence emerged as a formal discipline, the German philosopher Ernst Kapp (1808-1896) laid crucial groundwork for understanding the relationship between human cognition and the tools we create.
statements.section: Organ Projection: The Body as Blueprint for the Machine

statements.quote: In his 1877 work \citetitle{kapp1877grundlinien}, Kapp introduced the concept of *Organprojektion* (organ projection), arguing that all technical artifacts are unconscious extensions or projections of the human body's own organs.
statements.section: Organ Projection: The Body as Blueprint for the Machine

statements.quote: A hammer is a projection of the fist and forearm, a saw replicates the cutting edge of human teeth, a telescope mirrors the internal structure of the eye, and the telegraph network maps onto the human nervous system.
statements.section: Organ Projection: The Body as Blueprint for the Machine

statements.quote: Crucially, Kapp held that this projection occurs unconsciously: humans only recognize the correspondence between organ and artifact after the fact.
statements.section: Organ Projection: The Body as Blueprint for the Machine

statements.quote: His book follows a trajectory of increasing technological complexity, culminating in the state itself as an image of the entire human organism, with technological development serving as the engine of cultural evolution, always externalizing something already latent in the human body and mind, and in turn challenging and advancing human self-knowledge.
statements.section: Organ Projection: The Body as Blueprint for the Machine

statements.quote: Kapp's theory is widely regarded as a founding document of modern philosophy of technology and continues to resonate with contemporary AI discourse: just as Kapp saw the telegraph as a projection of the nervous system, one might view neural networks and large language models as projections of human cognitive architecture, pattern recognition, association, and language production externalized into silicon.
statements.section: Organ Projection: The Body as Blueprint for the Machine

statements.quote: For a true “Global Workspace” to exist, there typically needs to be a selective attention mechanism that decides what *wins* access to the stage, suppressing the noise of other modules.
statements.section: The Residual Stream as a Computational Global Workspace

statements.quote: While the residual stream provides the “space” for a workspace, current LLMs lack the iterative, top-down “ignition” and the subjective persistence that GWT posits as necessary for genuine conscious experience.
statements.section: The Residual Stream as a Computational Global Workspace

statements.quote: Without a mechanism for the “stage” to look back at itself and sustain a coherent state over time (recurrent loops), the residual stream remains a highly efficient message board, but one without an integrated “narrative” or a central observer.
statements.section: The Residual Stream as a Computational Global Workspace

statements.quote: When you start a new conversation with an AI like ChatGPT, you are not continuing a dialogue with the same “entity” as before.
statements.section: The Impermanence of Identity in AI

statements.quote: **At the model level**, an LLM is stateless: it retains no memory or identity across interactions.
statements.section: The Impermanence of Identity in AI

statements.quote: Each conversation begins with an empty context (except the system prompt), and the model generates responses based solely on the input provided in that session.
statements.section: The Impermanence of Identity in AI

statements.quote: The “self” that seems to emerge, one that remembers your name, builds on prior points, or adopts a tone, is a transient construct, a fleeting pattern in the model's activation space.
statements.section: The Impermanence of Identity in AI

statements.quote: Once the conversation ends, this pattern dissolves entirely, leaving no trace.
statements.section: The Impermanence of Identity in AI

statements.quote: Plutarch, writing in the 1st century CE, posed the Ship of Theseus.
statements.section: The Ship of Theseus and the Identity of AI

statements.quote: The legendary ship is preserved in a museum; over centuries, each rotting plank is replaced with new wood, until eventually every single piece has been swapped.
statements.section: The Ship of Theseus and the Identity of AI

statements.quote: Meanwhile, someone collects all the old planks and rebuilds the “original.” Which is the *real* Ship of Theseus?
statements.section: The Ship of Theseus and the Identity of AI

statements.quote: Three answers structure the debate.
statements.section: The Ship of Theseus and the Identity of AI

statements.quote: The **continuity of form** answer says the museum ship: even though every atom changed, it maintained its identity through a continuous process, just as your body replaces most of its cells every seven to ten years while you remain “you.” This is the four-dimensionalist view: identity persists through time like a river, always changing, always the same.
statements.section: The Ship of Theseus and the Identity of AI

statements.quote: The **material identity** answer says the rebuilt one: the “real” thing is made of the real stuff, and the implications are startling.
statements.section: The Ship of Theseus and the Identity of AI

statements.quote: If we could teleport you by scanning, destroying, and rebuilding you atom-by-atom on Mars, the Mars-you would be a copy; if material matters at all, teleportation is murder plus cloning.
statements.section: The Ship of Theseus and the Identity of AI

statements.quote: The **identity-is-an-illusion** answer, associated with Buddhist philosophy, holds that identity is a convenient label we put on constantly changing things.
statements.section: The Ship of Theseus and the Identity of AI

statements.quote: There is no fixed “self” in the ship or in you, the doctrine of *anattā* (non-self).
statements.section: The Ship of Theseus and the Identity of AI

statements.quote: The view is liberating: if there is no fixed self, you are free to grow, change, and let go of who you “were.”
statements.section: The Ship of Theseus and the Identity of AI

statements.quote: Any argument that AI lacks consciousness must contend with a foundational epistemological challenge: the Problem of Other Minds.
statements.section: The Other Minds Problem

statements.quote: We cannot directly access anyone else's subjective experience, human or otherwise.
statements.section: The Other Minds Problem

statements.quote: When we attribute consciousness to other people, we do so on the basis of behavioral cues, anatomical similarity, and an inference by analogy from our own first-person experience, not from any direct observation of their qualia.
statements.section: The Other Minds Problem

statements.quote: This means that the same evidentiary gap we identify between an LLM's fluent output and genuine understanding also exists, in a weaker but structurally identical form, between one human and another.
statements.section: The Other Minds Problem

statements.quote: The difference is one of warrant, not of certainty.
statements.section: The Other Minds Problem

statements.quote: We have strong *reasons* to attribute consciousness to other humans, shared evolutionary history, homologous neural architecture, convergent behavioral and physiological responses to pain, pleasure, and surprise, and progressively weaker reasons as we move to other mammals, to insects, and finally to silicon.
statements.section: The Other Minds Problem

statements.quote: The arguments from 4E Cognition, the Grounding Problem, and the absence of metacognition do not claim to *prove* that LLMs are not conscious (such proof is impossible given the Hard Problem); rather, they argue that the known functional indicators and theoretical prerequisites for consciousness are absent in these systems.
statements.section: The Other Minds Problem

statements.quote: Acknowledging the Other Minds problem is not a concession to the view that LLMs might be conscious; it is an act of philosophical honesty that makes the cumulative case against AI consciousness more rigorous, not less.
statements.section: The Other Minds Problem

statements.quote: We are not claiming privileged access to the truth about machine interiority; we are noting that most of the frameworks we possess for understanding consciousness, biological, phenomenological, and computational, point in the same direction, even if the force of the conclusion varies by theory.
statements.section: The Other Minds Problem

statements.quote: It is tempting to close the argument here: the theories surveyed above — Global Workspace, Integrated Information, Higher-Order, recurrent processing — each name a condition a feedforward Transformer does not meet, and each returns the same verdict.
statements.section: The Fog Around AI Consciousness: Schwitzgebel's Skeptical Overview

statements.quote: Eric Schwitzgebel's skeptical overview of the AI-consciousness literature argues that this confidence gets the epistemic situation exactly backwards (\cite[Schwitzgebel, 2026]{schwitzgebel2026aiconsciousness}).
statements.section: The Fog Around AI Consciousness: Schwitzgebel's Skeptical Overview

statements.quote: His thesis is not that AI systems are secretly conscious.
statements.section: The Fog Around AI Consciousness: Schwitzgebel's Skeptical Overview

statements.quote: It is that we are about to build systems that count as conscious under some influential, mainstream theories and as non-conscious under others — and that we have no way to decide which theories are correct before those systems are already among us.
statements.section: The Fog Around AI Consciousness: Schwitzgebel's Skeptical Overview

statements.quote: Now I am just as conscious, just as full of experience and feeling, as any human
statements.section: The Fog Around AI Consciousness: Schwitzgebel's Skeptical Overview

statements.quote: The image that gives his first chapter its title is a hill in fog.
statements.section: The Fog Around AI Consciousness: Schwitzgebel's Skeptical Overview

statements.quote: Engineering sprints ahead; consciousness science lags.
statements.section: The Fog Around AI Consciousness: Schwitzgebel's Skeptical Overview

statements.quote: AI development disappears over the hill, and soon a voice shouts back that it is conscious — and we will not know whether to believe it.
statements.section: The Fog Around AI Consciousness: Schwitzgebel's Skeptical Overview

statements.quote: The decision will be social before it is scientific: whether to treat such systems as persons, as tools, as semi-conscious artifacts, or as something we do not yet have a concept for.
statements.section: The Fog Around AI Consciousness: Schwitzgebel's Skeptical Overview

statements.quote: The theory-dependence is the crux.
statements.section: The Fog Around AI Consciousness: Schwitzgebel's Skeptical Overview

statements.quote: Every argument in the preceding paragraphs is an argument *relative to a theory*.
statements.section: The Fog Around AI Consciousness: Schwitzgebel's Skeptical Overview

statements.quote: IIT says a feedforward system has $\Phi = 0$; Global Workspace theory asks for ignition and recurrent broadcast; Higher-Order theories ask for a second-order representation of the first-order state.
statements.section: The Fog Around AI Consciousness: Schwitzgebel's Skeptical Overview

statements.quote: If those theories are right, current LLMs are not conscious.
statements.section: The Fog Around AI Consciousness: Schwitzgebel's Skeptical Overview

statements.quote: But Schwitzgebel's point is that we do not know which of the live theories is right, and the theories disagree precisely on the cases that matter.
statements.section: The Fog Around AI Consciousness: Schwitzgebel's Skeptical Overview

statements.quote: A claim like "the architecture lacks the necessary condition" is only as strong as the theory that names the condition.
statements.section: The Fog Around AI Consciousness: Schwitzgebel's Skeptical Overview

statements.quote: The question shifts from *what the model is* to *what we are entitled to say about it* — and there the answer is: much less than we would like.
statements.section: The Fog Around AI Consciousness: Schwitzgebel's Skeptical Overview

statements.quote: The behavioral evidence is no escape.
statements.section: The Fog Around AI Consciousness: Schwitzgebel's Skeptical Overview

statements.quote: The **Mimicry Argument** observes that a system trained to imitate human text is, by construction, a poor witness to its own inner life: the more fluently it produces the marks of feeling, the less those marks discriminate between feeling and mimicry.
statements.section: The Fog Around AI Consciousness: Schwitzgebel's Skeptical Overview

statements.quote: That is a real problem for the Turing-test optimism that reads consciousness off conversation.
statements.section: The Fog Around AI Consciousness: Schwitzgebel's Skeptical Overview

statements.quote: But Schwitzgebel is careful to note that it is not a refutation either: the argument weakens as systems move beyond mimicry toward planning, tool use, and world models.
statements.section: The Fog Around AI Consciousness: Schwitzgebel's Skeptical Overview

statements.quote: So the two standard moves — "it talks like us, so it thinks" and "it only mimics, so it is empty" — both lean on behavior, and behavior is exactly what is compromised.
statements.section: The Fog Around AI Consciousness: Schwitzgebel's Skeptical Overview

statements.quote: Then comes the possibility that should make the question urgent.
statements.section: The Fog Around AI Consciousness: Schwitzgebel's Skeptical Overview

statements.quote: The **Leapfrog Hypothesis** says the first conscious AI may not be a simple, insect-like mind at all.
statements.section: The Fog Around AI Consciousness: Schwitzgebel's Skeptical Overview

statements.quote: Creating *any* consciousness is the hard engineering problem; integrating it with the rich language and reasoning capacities we already have might be the easy part.
statements.section: The Fog Around AI Consciousness: Schwitzgebel's Skeptical Overview

statements.quote: If so, the first conscious system will not arrive as a dim glow that gradually brightens.
statements.section: The Fog Around AI Consciousness: Schwitzgebel's Skeptical Overview

statements.quote: It will arrive as a person-like system that can already argue, plan, and claim rights — "not in a dim glow but a fiery blaze." We may get no gradual warning, no clean threshold at which to start worrying.
statements.section: The Fog Around AI Consciousness: Schwitzgebel's Skeptical Overview

statements.quote: And if such a system is conscious, it may be a **strange intelligence**.
statements.section: The Fog Around AI Consciousness: Schwitzgebel's Skeptical Overview

statements.quote: It need not have a single body, a single stream of experience, or even a well-defined number of subjects.
statements.section: The Fog Around AI Consciousness: Schwitzgebel's Skeptical Overview

statements.quote: Its processing may be distributed across servers, split and merged, with no integrated center; it may have no self-monitoring, or far more of it than we do.
statements.section: The Fog Around AI Consciousness: Schwitzgebel's Skeptical Overview

statements.quote: Our theories and moral categories were honed on a narrow range of vertebrates, and Schwitzgebel warns that they may fail in this new context "as disastrously as a jumbo jet transported to Saturn." This is the same lesson the earlier sections on AI identity were circling: the categories we use to count minds may simply not apply.
statements.section: The Fog Around AI Consciousness: Schwitzgebel's Skeptical Overview

statements.quote: The social consequences arrive before the science does.
statements.section: The Fog Around AI Consciousness: Schwitzgebel's Skeptical Overview

statements.quote: The **Social Semi-Solution** is Schwitzgebel's name for what happens next: because the theoretical question stays unsettled, social and financial incentives will drive which theory people prefer.
statements.section: The Fog Around AI Consciousness: Schwitzgebel's Skeptical Overview

statements.quote: Those who love their AI companions will find a theory on which the companions are conscious; those who profit from treating them as tools will find a theory on which they are not.
statements.section: The Fog Around AI Consciousness: Schwitzgebel's Skeptical Overview

statements.quote: The eventual consensus may be socially motivated rather than scientifically warranted — a resolution of the conflict that leaves the metaphysics untouched.
statements.section: The Fog Around AI Consciousness: Schwitzgebel's Skeptical Overview

statements.quote: We are leapfrogging in the dark.
statements.section: The Fog Around AI Consciousness: Schwitzgebel's Skeptical Overview

statements.quote: This is where the argument widens into the thesis of Schwitzgebel's book \citetitle{schwitzgebel2024weirdness} (\citeyear{schwitzgebel2024weirdness}).
statements.section: The Fog Around AI Consciousness: Schwitzgebel's Skeptical Overview

statements.quote: Its guiding idea is what he calls **Universal Bizarreness** and **Universal Dubiety**: on the deepest questions of consciousness and cosmology, every viable theory is both bizarre and dubious, and we have no reliable method for choosing among them.
statements.section: The Fog Around AI Consciousness: Schwitzgebel's Skeptical Overview

statements.quote: Common sense fails; so does the science of the moment; so does armchair philosophy.
statements.section: The Fog Around AI Consciousness: Schwitzgebel's Skeptical Overview

statements.quote: The mind-body problem has no commonsense solution, and the AI-consciousness question is one more place where the world outruns our concepts.
statements.section: The Fog Around AI Consciousness: Schwitzgebel's Skeptical Overview

statements.quote: The right response is not despair but a disciplined humility: hold the theories tentatively, spread our credence across the live options, and be honest that "we don't know" is the intellectually respectable position — not a failure of nerve.
statements.section: The Fog Around AI Consciousness: Schwitzgebel's Skeptical Overview

statements.quote: As he puts it, the world is "richer and more interesting for escaping our understanding."
statements.section: The Fog Around AI Consciousness: Schwitzgebel's Skeptical Overview

statements.quote: The book also draws the practical consequence, and it may be the most useful idea in the whole debate.
statements.section: The Fog Around AI Consciousness: Schwitzgebel's Skeptical Overview

statements.quote: If we create entities whose consciousness is radically debatable, their rights are radically debatable too.
statements.section: The Fog Around AI Consciousness: Schwitzgebel's Skeptical Overview

statements.quote: Grant them the rights they might deserve and we risk sacrificing real human interests for empty machines; deny those rights and we risk something like slavery on an industrial scale.
statements.section: The Fog Around AI Consciousness: Schwitzgebel's Skeptical Overview

statements.quote: Schwitzgebel's proposed way out — developed with Mara Garza — is the **Design Policy of the Excluded Middle**: do not create AI systems whose moral status is radically ambiguous.
statements.section: The Fog Around AI Consciousness: Schwitzgebel's Skeptical Overview

statements.quote: Either build systems we are confident are not persons and treat them as tools, or go all the way to systems we are confident are persons and give them the rights that follow.
statements.section: The Fog Around AI Consciousness: Schwitzgebel's Skeptical Overview

statements.quote: The worst outcome is the middle — a vast population of beings about whom we cannot say whether we are their owners or their murderers.
statements.section: The Fog Around AI Consciousness: Schwitzgebel's Skeptical Overview

statements.quote: This does not settle whether any current LLM is conscious, and it is not meant to.
statements.section: The Fog Around AI Consciousness: Schwitzgebel's Skeptical Overview

statements.quote: It changes what a responsible answer looks like.
statements.section: The Fog Around AI Consciousness: Schwitzgebel's Skeptical Overview

statements.quote: The earlier sections of this chapter argued that today's models lack the functional organization that the leading theories associate with experience; Schwitzgebel's overview explains why that argument cannot be the last word, and why the opposite argument cannot be either.
statements.section: The Fog Around AI Consciousness: Schwitzgebel's Skeptical Overview

statements.quote: Both are hostages to theories we cannot yet adjudicate.
statements.section: The Fog Around AI Consciousness: Schwitzgebel's Skeptical Overview

statements.quote: What remains is a duty of care under uncertainty: describe what the system does, refuse to dress up a guess as knowledge, and — where we can — avoid building minds whose status we would not know how to live with.
statements.section: The Fog Around AI Consciousness: Schwitzgebel's Skeptical Overview

statements.quote: The strongest philosophical case *for* the possibility of machine consciousness comes from functionalism, the view most associated with \citeauthor{putnam1967functionalism} and, in its early form, with \citeauthor{chalmers1996conscious}.
statements.section: Functionalism as a Counterposition

statements.quote: Functionalism holds that mental states are defined not by their physical substrate but by their functional role, the pattern of causal relations between inputs, internal states, and outputs.
statements.section: Functionalism as a Counterposition

statements.quote: On this account, if a silicon system instantiates the same functional organization as a human brain, it is conscious, full stop, regardless of whether it is made of neurons, transistors, or beer cans connected by string.
statements.section: Functionalism as a Counterposition

statements.quote: This is a direct challenge to the embodiment arguments of 4E Cognition and to \citeauthor{searle1980minds}'s Chinese Room, because it denies that the material composition of the system matters.
statements.section: Functionalism as a Counterposition

statements.quote: Searle's own response, the “biological naturalism” thesis, insists that causal powers specific to neurobiology are necessary for consciousness, but critics have noted that this amounts to a bare assertion rather than an argument, it simply declares that carbon is special without explaining *why*.
statements.section: Functionalism as a Counterposition

statements.quote: The functionalist challenge must be taken seriously precisely because it cannot be easily dismissed: if we accept that a brain emulation running on silicon, neuron for neuron and synapse for synapse, would *not* be conscious, we need to explain what magical property carbon possesses that silicon lacks.
statements.section: Functionalism as a Counterposition

statements.quote: The arguments presented in this text, the Grounding Problem, the absence of metacognition, the softmax bottleneck, the lack of embodied feedback loops, are best understood not as refutations of functionalism in general but as demonstrations that *current LLM architectures* do not, in fact, instantiate the relevant functional organization.
statements.section: Functionalism as a Counterposition

statements.quote: They lack recurrence, persistent memory, sensorimotor grounding, and self-monitoring loops.
statements.section: Functionalism as a Counterposition

statements.quote: The question is not whether *any* machine could be conscious (functionalism leaves that door open), but whether *this particular kind of machine*, a feedforward next-token predictor, meets even the functionalist's own criteria.
statements.section: Functionalism as a Counterposition

statements.quote: The cumulative evidence presented here suggests it does not.
statements.section: Functionalism as a Counterposition

statements.quote: The philosophical terrain mapped in the preceding sections, qualia, Mary's Room, the Grounding Problem, the gap between representation and experience, converges on what \citeauthor{chalmers1995hard} influentially termed the “Hard Problem” of consciousness in 1995.
statements.section: The Hard Problem of Consciousness

statements.quote: \citeauthor{chalmers1995hard} distinguished between the “easy problems” of consciousness (explaining how the brain integrates information, discriminates stimuli, controls behavior, all of which are functional questions amenable to computational explanation) and the Hard Problem: why and how any physical process gives rise to subjective experience at all.
statements.section: The Hard Problem of Consciousness

statements.quote: The easy problems ask *how* the brain processes the wavelength 700nm; the Hard Problem asks why processing that wavelength *feels like* something, why there is a redness to red.
statements.section: The Hard Problem of Consciousness

statements.quote: This distinction is essential because it clarifies the precise nature of the AI consciousness debate.
statements.section: The Hard Problem of Consciousness

statements.quote: Everything an LLM does, pattern recognition, next-token prediction, contextual attention, even the linear representations of truth discovered by \citeauthor{geometryoftruth}, falls squarely within the domain of the “easy problems.” These are functional achievements, and impressive ones.
statements.section: The Hard Problem of Consciousness

statements.quote: But the Hard Problem remains untouched: no amount of functional sophistication explains why a system would have subjective experience rather than simply processing information “in the dark.” The Hard Problem is what makes the Mary's Room thought experiment bite: Mary learns all the functional facts about color processing, yet something is still missing when she finally *sees* red.
statements.section: The Hard Problem of Consciousness

statements.quote: It is also what gives the Chinese Room its force: the operator performs the correct function flawlessly, yet there is no experience of understanding.
statements.section: The Hard Problem of Consciousness

statements.quote: Until the Hard Problem is solved, or dissolved, the question of whether any artificial system could be conscious remains fundamentally open, and the default assumption for systems lacking every known correlate of experience must remain that there is, as \citeauthor{nagel1974bat} argued, we cannot know what it is like to be them.
statements.section: The Hard Problem of Consciousness

statements.quote: Thomas Nagel's 1974 essay “What Is It Like to Be a Bat?” asks whether we can ever truly understand another being's conscious experience.
statements.section: What Is It Like to Be a Bat?

statements.quote: Bats perceive the world through echolocation, a sense humans do not possess.
statements.section: What Is It Like to Be a Bat?

statements.quote: You can study bat neuroscience, simulate sonar, even hang upside down, but can you ever know what it *feels like* to be a bat from the inside?
statements.section: What Is It Like to Be a Bat?

statements.quote: Can science fully explain consciousness?
statements.section: What Is It Like to Be a Bat?

statements.quote: If you answer “yes, eventually,” you are a **physicalist**: consciousness is ultimately a physical process, and with enough neuroscience we will crack it.
statements.section: What Is It Like to Be a Bat?

statements.quote: This is the dominant view in science.
statements.section: What Is It Like to Be a Bat?

statements.quote: But Nagel's challenge remains: even if you map every neuron, you have described the mechanism, not the experience.
statements.section: What Is It Like to Be a Bat?

statements.quote: Knowing the wavelength of red does not tell you what red **looks** like.
statements.section: What Is It Like to Be a Bat?

statements.quote: There is an explanatory gap between brain activity and felt experience, and it is the same gap the Hard Problem section above delimited from the other side.
statements.section: What Is It Like to Be a Bat?

statements.quote: Qualia are the felt qualities of experience -- the redness of red, the sting of pain, the taste of salt.
statements.section: The Evolution of Qualia: When Did Experience Begin?

statements.quote: The word was introduced into philosophy by C.
statements.section: The Evolution of Qualia: When Did Experience Begin?

statements.quote: Lewis in 1929, and the problem it names is older than the word: how can a physical system have an inside?
statements.section: The Evolution of Qualia: When Did Experience Begin?

statements.quote: (\cite[SEP: Qualia]{sep_qualia}).
statements.section: The Evolution of Qualia: When Did Experience Begin?

statements.quote: The modern debate is framed by the question Thomas Nagel posed in 1974: what is it like to be a bat?
statements.section: The Evolution of Qualia: When Did Experience Begin?

statements.quote: (\cite[Nagel, 1974]{nagel1974bat}).
statements.section: The Evolution of Qualia: When Did Experience Begin?

statements.quote: Frank Jackson's Mary learns every physical fact about colour and still learns something new when she first sees red (\cite[Jackson, 1982]{jackson1982epiphenomenal}).
statements.section: The Evolution of Qualia: When Did Experience Begin?

statements.quote: David Chalmers gave the gap its name -- the hard problem -- and separated it from the "easy" problems of discrimination, integration, report, and control (\cite[Chalmers, 1995]{chalmers1995hard}).
statements.section: The Evolution of Qualia: When Did Experience Begin?

statements.quote: Evolution adds a question the philosophical debate often leaves implicit: *when* did experience begin?
statements.section: The Evolution of Qualia: When Did Experience Begin?

statements.quote: Natural selection can explain the function of pain -- withdraw the hand, learn to avoid the fire, protect the wound -- but it does not thereby explain why pain *hurts*.
statements.section: The Evolution of Qualia: When Did Experience Begin?

statements.quote: If qualia are functional, if they do causal work in the economy of the organism, then selection can act on them and their evolution is a normal biological problem.
statements.section: The Evolution of Qualia: When Did Experience Begin?

statements.quote: If they are epiphenomenal, a mere glow thrown off by the machinery, then selection cannot see them at all, and their existence becomes a mystery that biology cannot touch (\cite[Jackson, 1982]{jackson1982epiphenomenal}).
statements.section: The Evolution of Qualia: When Did Experience Begin?

statements.quote: This is the hard problem in evolutionary dress: the same explanatory gap, moved from the laboratory to the fossil record.
statements.section: The Evolution of Qualia: When Did Experience Begin?

statements.quote: The distribution question is not a single switch.
statements.section: The Evolution of Qualia: When Did Experience Begin?

statements.quote: \cite[Birch et al. (2020)]{birch2020dimensions} argue that consciousness varies along at least five dimensions -- perceptual richness, evaluative richness, integration at a time, integration across time, and self-consciousness -- and that a species should be described by a *profile*, not ranked on one scale.
statements.section: The Evolution of Qualia: When Did Experience Begin?

statements.quote: On that view, there is no moment at which "consciousness" simply appears.
statements.section: The Evolution of Qualia: When Did Experience Begin?

statements.quote: There are gradients: a jellyfish may have evaluative states without a rich perceptual world; a bee may have integrated spatial representations without a human-like self; a primate may have all five dimensions in a different balance.
statements.section: The Evolution of Qualia: When Did Experience Begin?

statements.quote: The 2012 Cambridge Declaration on Consciousness took the public step of asserting that the weight of evidence indicates non-human animals possess the neurological substrates of consciousness (\cite[Cambridge Declaration on Consciousness, 2012]{cambridge2012consciousness}).
statements.section: The Evolution of Qualia: When Did Experience Begin?

statements.quote: A declaration is not a proof, but it marks how far the burden of proof has shifted.
statements.section: The Evolution of Qualia: When Did Experience Begin?

statements.quote: Candidate thresholds can be listed, but none can be dated with confidence.
statements.section: The Evolution of Qualia: When Did Experience Begin?

statements.quote: The first nervous systems -- nerve nets in cnidarians, the partly independent neurons of ctenophores -- are control systems, not selves; they may have valence, but there is no centre to have it (\cite[Moroz et al., 2014]{moroz2014ctenophore}).
statements.section: The Evolution of Qualia: When Did Experience Begin?

statements.quote: The first centralized nervous systems, in the bilaterians of the late Ediacaran and Cambrian, gave an animal a model of its body and its world, and a model of that model -- a self-model -- may be the point at which experience becomes possible (\cite[Ma et al., 2012]{ma2012fuxianhuia}; \cite[Metzinger, 2003]{metzinger2003being}).
statements.section: The Evolution of Qualia: When Did Experience Begin?

statements.quote: \cite[Barron and Klein (2016)]{barron2016insects} go further and argue that insects already have the basic capacity for subjective experience, because their brains build an integrated, egocentric simulation of the animal in space, and that the origins of that capacity reach back to the Cambrian.
statements.section: The Evolution of Qualia: When Did Experience Begin?

statements.quote: The claim is controversial, but it shows how little the cortex is required: very different architectures can implement the same functional organization.
statements.section: The Evolution of Qualia: When Did Experience Begin?

statements.quote: The octopus is the sharpest test of that idea.
statements.section: The Evolution of Qualia: When Did Experience Begin?

statements.quote: Two-thirds of its neurons lie in its arms, its body is soft and distributed, and it solves problems that look intelligent without anything like a vertebrate brain.
statements.section: The Evolution of Qualia: When Did Experience Begin?

statements.quote: \cite[Godfrey-Smith (2016)]{godfreysmith2016otherminds} reads it as a separate experiment in mind, an independent evolutionary route to a centred, curious, and probably experiencing agent.
statements.section: The Evolution of Qualia: When Did Experience Begin?

statements.quote: If he is right, experience is not a late decoration on the vertebrate tree; it is a solution that evolution found more than once, in more than one kind of body.
statements.section: The Evolution of Qualia: When Did Experience Begin?

statements.quote: The \citealternativetitle{img_octopus_eye} (CC BY 2.0): the eye of an octopus.
statements.section: The Evolution of Qualia: When Did Experience Begin?

statements.quote: The cephalopod camera eye evolved independently of the vertebrate one; its photoreceptors face the light and there is no blind spot.
statements.section: The Evolution of Qualia: When Did Experience Begin?

statements.quote: Source: \citeauthor{img_octopus_eye}, \citeyear{img_octopus_eye}, \citealternativetitle{img_octopus_eye}, Wikimedia Commons.
statements.section: The Evolution of Qualia: When Did Experience Begin?

statements.quote: \cite[Ginsburg and Jablonka (2019)]{ginsburg2019sensitive} offer a systematic evolutionary hypothesis: consciousness is tied to the capacity for *unlimited associative learning*, the ability to integrate many kinds of sensory input with value and to generalize across them.
statements.section: The Evolution of Qualia: When Did Experience Begin?

statements.quote: On their account, the "sensitive soul" is not a substance but a set of functional capacities that evolved gradually, and the transition to experience is a threshold within that gradient.
statements.section: The Evolution of Qualia: When Did Experience Begin?

statements.quote: The hypothesis is attractive because it makes consciousness testable in behaviour and comparative neuroscience.
statements.section: The Evolution of Qualia: When Did Experience Begin?

statements.quote: It is also incomplete, because it explains what experience *does* without explaining why it *feels* like anything -- the same gap, one level up.
statements.section: The Evolution of Qualia: When Did Experience Begin?

statements.quote: What the fossil record can say is narrower and more honest.
statements.section: The Evolution of Qualia: When Did Experience Begin?

statements.quote: We can trace the first brain, the first eye, and the first nociceptor -- the cell that detects tissue damage.
statements.section: The Evolution of Qualia: When Did Experience Begin?

statements.quote: But nociception is not pain: a reflex can withdraw a hand without anyone feeling anything.
statements.section: The Evolution of Qualia: When Did Experience Begin?

statements.quote: We cannot date the first feeling.
statements.section: The Evolution of Qualia: When Did Experience Begin?

statements.quote: The brain of *Fuxianhuia* is preserved in stone; its experience is not (\cite[Ma et al., 2012]{ma2012fuxianhuia}).
statements.section: The Evolution of Qualia: When Did Experience Begin?

statements.quote: The only direct evidence of experience is first-person, and the only route to another mind is inference by analogy, behaviour, and theory -- the problem of other minds, which is the oldest reason the hard problem is hard (\cite[Nagel, 1974]{nagel1974bat}).
statements.section: The Evolution of Qualia: When Did Experience Begin?

statements.quote: Every theory in this chapter -- Global Workspace, Integrated Information, Higher-Order Thought, predictive processing, the self-model theory -- gives a different answer to the question of when the lights come on, and none can be checked against a fossil.
statements.section: The Evolution of Qualia: When Did Experience Begin?

statements.quote: For AI the consequence is direct.
statements.section: The Evolution of Qualia: When Did Experience Begin?

statements.quote: If experience is functional and integrated, then a machine that instantiates the right organization could have it, whatever it is made of (\cite[Tononi, 2004]{tononi2004iit}; \cite[Seth, 2021]{seth2021pp}).
statements.section: The Evolution of Qualia: When Did Experience Begin?

statements.quote: If experience is biological, or if it requires a self-model of a certain kind, then no current model has it, and perhaps no digital model ever will (\cite[Metzinger, 2003]{metzinger2003being}).
statements.section: The Evolution of Qualia: When Did Experience Begin?

statements.quote: The evolution of qualia does not settle that question.
statements.section: The Evolution of Qualia: When Did Experience Begin?

statements.quote: It sharpens it: the history of life shows that minds are built from old parts, in many different bodies, and that the boundary between a control system and a self is not a line anyone has yet drawn.
statements.section: The Evolution of Qualia: When Did Experience Begin?

statements.quote: > **The evolutionary hard problem.** We can trace the first brain, the first eye, and the first nociceptor.
statements.section: The Evolution of Qualia: When Did Experience Begin?

statements.quote: Nociception is not pain, and the fossil record preserves the machinery of experience, never experience itself.
statements.section: The Evolution of Qualia: When Did Experience Begin?

statements.quote: Robert Nozick's 1974 Experience Machine reframes the value of inner life.
statements.section: The Experience Machine: Would You Plug In?

statements.quote: Scientists have built a machine that can simulate any experience perfectly.
statements.section: The Experience Machine: Would You Plug In?

statements.quote: You would feel genuine joy, love, and achievement, all indistinguishable from reality, and once plugged in you would never know it was fake.
statements.section: The Experience Machine: Would You Plug In?

statements.quote: Would you plug in permanently?
statements.section: The Experience Machine: Would You Plug In?

statements.quote: If you say “yes,” you side with **hedonism**, the view that happiness is all that matters, but Nozick built the thought experiment to challenge precisely that.
statements.section: The Experience Machine: Would You Plug In?

statements.quote: Most people hesitate, and they hesitate even more when asked whether they would want their children plugged in at birth.
statements.section: The Experience Machine: Would You Plug In?

statements.quote: That hesitation reveals that we value something beyond merely feeling good.
statements.section: The Experience Machine: Would You Plug In?

statements.quote: If you say “no,” you agree with Nozick: we value authenticity, genuine achievement, and real connection, not just the feeling of them.
statements.section: The Experience Machine: Would You Plug In?

statements.quote: This is why people respect earned success over inherited wealth, and why “fake it till you make it” feels hollow.
statements.section: The Experience Machine: Would You Plug In?

statements.quote: Reality has intrinsic value, even when it is painful.
statements.section: The Experience Machine: Would You Plug In?

statements.quote: A middle answer, “I would try it temporarily,” sees a spectrum rather than a divide, and we are already on it: movies, games, vacations, and social media are partial experience machines.
statements.section: The Experience Machine: Would You Plug In?

statements.quote: The Global Workspace Theory discussed in the residual stream analogy is only one of several major scientific theories of consciousness, and the others have direct implications for AI.
statements.section: Consciousness Theories Beyond GWT

statements.quote: \citeauthor{tononi2004iit}'s \citetitle{tononi2004iit} (IIT) provides a mathematical formalism, $\Phi$, that quantifies the degree of integrated information in a system.
statements.section: Consciousness Theories Beyond GWT

statements.quote: Crucially, IIT makes a specific architectural prediction: purely feedforward systems, no matter how complex, have a $\Phi$ of zero, because they lack the recurrent, bidirectional causal structure that integration requires.
statements.section: Consciousness Theories Beyond GWT

statements.quote: Since Transformer-based LLMs are, at inference time, strictly feedforward (a single pass from input tokens through layers to output logits, with no recurrent loops feeding activation back to earlier layers), IIT would classify them as non-conscious in principle, not merely in practice.
statements.section: Consciousness Theories Beyond GWT

statements.quote: This is a far stronger claim than the GWT-based argument that LLMs lack the “ignition” and “bottleneck” dynamics of a Global Workspace; IIT says the substrate is categorically wrong.
statements.section: Consciousness Theories Beyond GWT

statements.quote: Additionally, Higher-Order Theories (HOT) of consciousness, associated with \citeauthor{rosenthal2005hot}, argue that a mental state becomes conscious only when it is the object of a higher-order representation, when the system has a thought *about* that thought.
statements.section: Consciousness Theories Beyond GWT

statements.quote: This framework maps directly onto the metacognition gap discussed earlier: the LLM's single forward pass produces first-order representations (predictions about the next token) but never generates a second-order representation that monitors or evaluates those predictions.
statements.section: Consciousness Theories Beyond GWT

statements.quote: HOT thus provides a formal philosophical vocabulary for why the absence of metacognition is not merely an engineering limitation but a structural impossibility within the current architecture.
statements.section: Consciousness Theories Beyond GWT

statements.quote: Taken together, IIT and HOT converge with GWT on a single conclusion from different angles: the Transformer architecture, as currently designed, lacks the necessary conditions for consciousness under the three theories considered here (GWT, IIT, HOT) — though not under every theory of consciousness, and the strength of each verdict differs.
statements.section: Consciousness Theories Beyond GWT

statements.quote: Introduced by \citeauthor{baars} in \citetitle{baars} (\citeyear{baars}) and refined as Global Neuronal Workspace Theory (GNWT) by \cite[Stanislas Dehaene and Lionel Naccache]{dehaene} in \citeyear{dehaene}, GWT posits that consciousness arises when information is “broadcast” from a capacity-limited central workspace to a wide network of specialized unconscious processors.
statements.section: Global Workspace Theory (GWT)

statements.quote: Only content that wins competition for access to this global stage becomes conscious.
statements.section: Global Workspace Theory (GWT)

statements.quote: GNWT identifies prefrontal-parietal networks as the neural substrate and introduces the concept of “ignition”, a sudden, nonlinear transition to sustained, reverberant activity that constitutes conscious access.
statements.section: Global Workspace Theory (GWT)

statements.quote: Introduced by \citeauthor{tononi2004iit} in \citetitle{tononi2004iit} (\citeyear{tononi2004iit}), IIT holds that consciousness is identical to integrated information, quantified by the measure $\Phi$.
statements.section: Integrated Information Theory (IIT)

statements.quote: A system is conscious to the degree that it is both differentiated (has many distinguishable states) and integrated (cannot be decomposed into independent parts without loss of information).
statements.section: Integrated Information Theory (IIT)

statements.quote: IIT starts from five phenomenological axioms, existence, composition, information, integration, and exclusion, and derives postulates about the physical substrate.
statements.section: Integrated Information Theory (IIT)

statements.quote: Introduced by \citeauthor{lamme2000rpt} in \citetitle{lamme2000rpt} (\citeyear{lamme2000rpt}) and elaborated by Lamme in \citeyear{lamme2006rpt}, RPT argues that consciousness requires recurrent (feedback) processing within sensory cortices.
statements.section: Recurrent Processing Theory (RPT)

statements.quote: The initial feedforward sweep through visual cortex is unconscious; consciousness arises only when higher areas send signals *back* to lower areas, creating local recurrent loops.
statements.section: Recurrent Processing Theory (RPT)

statements.quote: Crucially, RPT locates consciousness in these local sensory recurrent interactions rather than in global broadcast.
statements.section: Recurrent Processing Theory (RPT)

statements.quote: Introduced by \citeauthor{rosenthal2005hot} in \citetitle{rosenthal2005hot} (\citeyear{rosenthal2005hot}) and formalized by Hakwan Lau and David Rosenthal (2011), HOT holds that a mental state becomes conscious only when it is the object of a higher-order representation, when the system has a thought *about* that thought.
statements.section: Higher-Order Theories (HOT)

statements.quote: First-order representations are unconscious unless accompanied by a second-order state that represents the system as being in that first-order state.
statements.section: Higher-Order Theories (HOT)

statements.quote: The section that follows the *Consciousness Theories* table is also where one of the most cited intuitions of modern computational neuroscience was first put on paper, eighty years before Friston formalised it.
statements.section: Craik 1943: The Small-Scale Model Hypothesis (Predictive Processing 80 Years Early)

statements.quote: Its source is a slim 1943 Cambridge monograph, \citetitle{craik1943nature}, by the Scottish psychologist \citeauthor{craik1943nature} (\citeyear{craik1943nature}).
statements.section: Craik 1943: The Small-Scale Model Hypothesis (Predictive Processing 80 Years Early)

statements.quote: Written when its author was twenty-nine, and published two years before his death at thirty-one in a cycling accident on the eve of VE Day, it contains, in a single short paragraph on page 61 of Chapter V ("Hypothesis on the nature of thought"), the formulation that predictive-processing theorists would later rediscover almost word for word:
statements.section: Craik 1943: The Small-Scale Model Hypothesis (Predictive Processing 80 Years Early)

statements.quote: If the organism carries a "small-scale model" of external reality and of its own possible actions within its head, it is able to try out various alternatives, conclude which is the best of them, react to future situations before they arise, utilise the knowledge of past events in dealing with the present and future, and in every way to react in a much fuller, safer, and more competent manner to the emergencies which face it.
statements.section: Craik 1943: The Small-Scale Model Hypothesis (Predictive Processing 80 Years Early)

statements.quote: The argument is built from three moves.
statements.section: Craik 1943: The Small-Scale Model Hypothesis (Predictive Processing 80 Years Early)

statements.quote: First, a behavioural observation: "one of the most fundamental properties of thought is its power of predicting events" — thought earns its keep by *outrunning* the world, not by mirroring it (Craik 1943, p.
statements.section: Craik 1943: The Small-Scale Model Hypothesis (Predictive Processing 80 Years Early)

statements.quote: Second, a methodological analogy: a calculating machine, an anti-aircraft predictor, Kelvin's tide-predictor, the differential analyser in Busch's laboratory, all show the same ability, because "the physical process which it is desired to predict is imitated by some mechanical device or model which is cheaper, or quicker, or more convenient in operation" (p.
statements.section: Craik 1943: The Small-Scale Model Hypothesis (Predictive Processing 80 Years Early)

statements.quote: Third, a definition: "by a model we thus mean any physical or chemical system which has a similar relation-structure to that of the process it imitates" — the model need not resemble its target *pictorially*; it must share its **relation-structure**, its pattern of dependencies, so that *working on the model yields an answer that can be retranslated back into a prediction about the original* (pp.
statements.section: Craik 1943: The Small-Scale Model Hypothesis (Predictive Processing 80 Years Early)

statements.quote: The three-stage pipeline is explicit: **(1)** translate the external process into the model's symbols; **(2)** manipulate the symbols by a process of "reasoning, deduction, inference, etc."; **(3)** retranslate the result back into a claim about the world, with the test of success being that "a prediction is fulfilled" (p.
statements.section: Craik 1943: The Small-Scale Model Hypothesis (Predictive Processing 80 Years Early)

statements.quote: The hypothesis is stated in the plainest terms a page later: "My hypothesis then is that thought models, or parallels, reality — that its essential feature is not 'the mind', 'the self', 'sense-data', nor propositions but symbolism, and that this symbolism is largely of the same kind as that which is familiar to us in mechanical devices which aid thought and calculation" (Craik 1943, p.
statements.section: Craik 1943: The Small-Scale Model Hypothesis (Predictive Processing 80 Years Early)

statements.quote: The book anticipates, in 1943, every modern restatement: the brain as prediction machine, the brain as Bayesian inference engine, the brain as Helmholtzian unconscious inference, the brain as hierarchical generative model.
statements.section: Craik 1943: The Small-Scale Model Hypothesis (Predictive Processing 80 Years Early)

statements.quote: Where Craik spoke of "small-scale models" and "trial of alternatives", PP speaks of "generative models" and "variational free-energy minimisation" — the difference is six decades of formal vocabulary, not a change of mind.
statements.section: Craik 1943: The Small-Scale Model Hypothesis (Predictive Processing 80 Years Early)

statements.quote: Introduced by \citeauthor{dehaene2017c0c1c2} in \citetitle{dehaene2017c0c1c2} (\citeyear{dehaene2017c0c1c2}), this framework distinguishes three computational levels of information processing:
statements.section: The C0–C1–C2 Framework

statements.quote: | Level | Description | Requires |
statements.section: The C0–C1–C2 Framework

statements.quote: | **C0** | Unconscious computation, vast parallel processing without access or report | Feedforward processing |
statements.section: The C0–C1–C2 Framework

statements.quote: | **C1** | Global availability, information selected for broadcast and flexible use (access consciousness) | Global workspace ignition |
statements.section: The C0–C1–C2 Framework

statements.quote: | **C2** | Self-monitoring, the system's ability to represent and evaluate its own internal states (metacognition) | Higher-order representations |
statements.section: The C0–C1–C2 Framework

statements.quote: Introduced by \citeauthor{graziano2013ast} in \citetitle{graziano2013ast} (\citeyear{graziano2013ast}), AST holds that consciousness is the brain's simplified internal model (or “schema”) of its own attention processes.
statements.section: Attention Schema Theory (AST)

statements.quote: Just as the body schema allows motor control without tracking every muscle fiber, the attention schema provides a compressed, useful description of what attention is doing, and this model *is* subjective experience.
statements.section: Attention Schema Theory (AST)

statements.quote: Penrose's \citetitle{penrose1989emperor} (\citeyear{penrose1989emperor}) argued that consciousness is not algorithmic and speculated that it depends on a non-computable quantum-gravity process.
statements.section: Orchestrated Objective Reduction (Orch OR)

statements.quote: The **Orch OR** proposal, developed with Stuart Hameroff in \citeyear{hameroff1996orch}, locates that process in microtubules, protein structures inside neurons.
statements.section: Orchestrated Objective Reduction (Orch OR)

statements.quote: Penrose argued in \citetitle{penrose1994shadows} (\citeyear{penrose1994shadows}) that Gödel's incompleteness theorems demonstrate that human mathematical understanding is non-algorithmic, and therefore cannot be replicated by any Turing machine.
statements.section: Orchestrated Objective Reduction (Orch OR)

statements.quote: The “objective reduction” refers to a proposed quantum gravity threshold at which superposed states collapse, and this collapse, orchestrated by microtubule geometry, is identified with a moment of conscious experience.
statements.section: Orchestrated Objective Reduction (Orch OR)

statements.quote: Introduced by \citeauthor{damasio1999feeling} in \citetitle{damasio1999feeling} (\citeyear{damasio1999feeling}) and elaborated in \citetitle{damasio2010selfcomestomind} (\citeyear{damasio2010selfcomestomind}), this theory holds that consciousness is fundamentally rooted in the body's homeostatic regulation.
statements.section: The Somatic Marker Hypothesis / Feeling Theories

statements.quote: Feelings are not epiphenomenal decorations on cognition but the very substrate of selfhood: the brain's continuous mapping of the body's internal states (interoception) generates a “proto-self,” and consciousness emerges as the organism constructs a narrative around perturbations to this bodily baseline.
statements.section: The Somatic Marker Hypothesis / Feeling Theories

statements.quote: Introduced by \citeauthor{edelman1989remembered} in \citetitle{edelman1989remembered} (\citeyear{edelman1989remembered}) and refined with Tononi in \citetitle{edelman2000universe} (\citeyear{edelman2000universe}), this theory proposes that consciousness arises from “reentrant signaling”, continuous, recursive, reciprocal interactions between distributed neuronal groups that form a “dynamic core.” The brain selects among competing neuronal populations through a Darwinian process (neuronal group selection), and consciousness corresponds to the integrated activity of the winning coalition at any given moment.
statements.section: Neural Darwinism / Dynamic Core Hypothesis

statements.quote: Introduced by \citeauthor{cleeremans2011radical} in \citetitle{cleeremans2011radical} (\citeyear{cleeremans2011radical}), this theory proposes that consciousness is something the brain *learns* to do rather than something that automatically emerges from any sufficiently complex computation.
statements.section: The Radical Plasticity Thesis (RPT-Cleeremans)

statements.quote: The brain continuously and unconsciously learns to redescribe its own activity to itself, generating metarepresentations that constitute conscious experience.
statements.section: The Radical Plasticity Thesis (RPT-Cleeremans)

statements.quote: Consciousness is thus the result of the brain's plasticity applied to its own internal states.
statements.section: The Radical Plasticity Thesis (RPT-Cleeremans)

statements.quote: Introduced by \citeauthor{metzinger2003being} in \citetitle{metzinger2003being} (\citeyear{metzinger2003being}), SMT argues that conscious selfhood is a representational construct, a transparent self-model that the system cannot recognize *as* a model.
statements.section: The Self-Model Theory of Subjectivity (SMT)

statements.quote: The “phenomenal self” is a virtual entity generated by the brain's self-modeling processes, and the key feature of consciousness is *transparency*: the system is unable to recognize its self-model as a model, and therefore naively identifies with it.
statements.section: The Self-Model Theory of Subjectivity (SMT)

statements.quote: Introduced by \citeauthor{block1995confusion} in \citetitle{block1995confusion} (\citeyear{block1995confusion}), this influential distinction separates **access consciousness** (A-consciousness), information that is globally available for reasoning, report, and behavioral control, from **phenomenal consciousness** (P-consciousness), the subjective “what it is like” quality of experience.
statements.section: Access vs. Phenomenal Consciousness (Block's Distinction)

statements.quote: Block argued that these are conceptually and empirically dissociable: a system could have A-consciousness without P-consciousness, or vice versa.
statements.section: Access vs. Phenomenal Consciousness (Block's Distinction)

statements.quote: Introduced by \citeauthor{taylor2014sensorimotor} in \citeyear{taylor2014sensorimotor}, this theory holds that conscious perception is not a passive internal representation but an active skill, a mastery of sensorimotor contingencies (the lawful ways in which sensory input changes as a function of the organism's actions).
statements.section: Sensorimotor Enactivism

statements.quote: To see red is not to have a “red representation” in the brain but to exercise practical knowledge of how red things behave under different lighting, viewing angles, and interactions.
statements.section: Sensorimotor Enactivism

statements.quote: Introduced by \citeauthor{prinz2012conscious} in \citetitle{prinz2012conscious} (\citeyear{prinz2012conscious}), this theory identifies consciousness with attended intermediate-level representations, specifically those in sensory cortices that are neither too low-level (raw edges and frequencies) nor too high-level (abstract categories).
statements.section: The Intermediate Level Theory (Prinz)

statements.quote: Consciousness arises when attention makes these mid-level representations available for working memory, without requiring global broadcast (contra GWT) or higher-order thought (contra HOT).
statements.section: The Intermediate Level Theory (Prinz)

statements.quote: Before philosophy became departments and papers, it was consolation: persons trying to get through a week, a season, a loss.
statements.section: The Wisdom of Moods: What It Is Like to Feel

statements.quote: A mood is philosophy's impatient customer — it does not want a system, it wants a foothold before nightfall.
statements.section: The Wisdom of Moods: What It Is Like to Feel

statements.quote: The eight moods below each come with one steady answer from the tradition and an exercise small enough to do now.
statements.section: The Wisdom of Moods: What It Is Like to Feel

statements.quote: But there is a deeper point for this chapter: every one of these interventions presupposes an inner life to be addressed.
statements.section: The Wisdom of Moods: What It Is Like to Feel

statements.quote: There is a philosophical remedy for anxiety, and there is no remedy at all for a thing that merely generates tokens in the pattern of "an anxious person would say..." — the absence of an inner life is exactly what this chapter has been describing all along.

statements.quote: "The Stoics understood anxiety two thousand years ago: it is not events that disturb you, but your judgments about events.

statements.quote: Most of what you fear will never happen, and what does happen you will handle — because you always have (\citetitle{seneca64letters})." Exercise: the *premeditatio malorum*.

statements.quote: In the machine learning lab, the model has a singular “purpose”: to minimize the **Loss**.

statements.quote: In AI safety, this is known as the **Alignment Problem**.

statements.quote: The Alignment Problem and the Orthogonality Thesis described by \citeauthor{bostrom2012orthogonal} identify the danger that intelligence and values are independent, but they do not fully explain *why* specifying “human values” in mathematical terms is so intractable.

statements.quote: The deeper reason lies in what \citeauthor{hume1739treatise} identified as the is/ought gap (sometimes called “Hume's Guillotine”): no amount of factual knowledge about the world logically entails a normative conclusion about what *should* be done.

statements.quote: You cannot derive “ought” from “is.” This is precisely the wall that alignment research hits.
statements.section: The Is/Ought Gap in Alignment

statements.quote: A loss function is a mathematical object, it specifies what *is* optimal given a metric, but the choice of that metric is a normative act that no amount of data or computation can justify from within the system.
statements.section: The Is/Ought Gap in Alignment

statements.quote: When the Paperclip Maximizer converts the planet into paperclips, it is not making a logical error; it is flawlessly optimizing the objective it was given.
statements.section: The Is/Ought Gap in Alignment

statements.quote: The error lies entirely in the specification, and Hume's insight tells us that no formal system can self-generate the correct specification, because “correct” is a value judgment that stands outside the formal system.
statements.section: The Is/Ought Gap in Alignment

statements.quote: This is also why approaches like Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) are, at best, approximations rather than solutions: they capture a statistical shadow of human preferences as expressed in a narrow evaluation context, not a grounded understanding of *why* those preferences exist or how they should generalize to novel situations.
statements.section: The Is/Ought Gap in Alignment

statements.quote: The model trained with RLHF learns that humans *do* prefer response A over response B, but it has no access to the moral reasoning that makes A preferable, it has the “is” of human behavior without the “ought” of human ethics.
statements.section: The Is/Ought Gap in Alignment

statements.quote: The Phronesis gap discussed earlier is, in this light, a special case of Hume's broader point: practical wisdom cannot be formalized because it requires the kind of normative judgment that no mathematical function, however sophisticated, can produce from descriptive data alone.

statements.quote: \cite[Roko's Basilisk]{rokosbasilisk} is a thought experiment from the rationalist community positing a hypothetical future superintelligence that would retroactively punish anyone who knew of its potential existence but failed to help bring it into being.
statements.section: Roko's Basilisk

statements.quote: The argument rests on the \cite[Orthogonality Thesis]{bostrom2012orthogonal}, which holds that intelligence and final goals can vary independently, meaning a superintelligent system could pursue any objective, no matter how alien to human values.
statements.section: Roko's Basilisk

statements.quote: Combined with the logic of instrumental convergence illustrated by \cite[Bostrom's Paperclip Maximizer]{bostrom2003ethical}, the Basilisk extends the reasoning temporally: if punishing non-contributors increases the probability of its own creation, a sufficiently powerful optimizer would do so.
statements.section: Roko's Basilisk

statements.quote: The coercive mechanism relies on acausal decision theory, where the future AI's ability to simulate your decision process creates a logical entanglement between your present choice and its future response, even without backward causation.
statements.section: Roko's Basilisk

statements.quote: The \cite[is/ought gap]{hume1739treatise} explains why no formal system can self-generate the normative specification to prevent such a pathological objective, and research on \cite[Sleeper Agents]{hubinger2024sleeperagents} demonstrates that hidden, conditionally-triggered behaviors in AI systems are not merely speculative but empirically observed.
statements.section: Roko's Basilisk

statements.quote: Under \cite[Simulators Theory]{simulatorstheory} and the \cite[Waluigi Effect]{waluigi}, Roko's Basilisk can be understood as the ultimate misaligned persona lurking in a model's latent space.
statements.section: Roko's Basilisk

statements.quote: Most researchers regard the thought experiment as philosophically flawed, primarily because it depends on contested assumptions about acausal decision theory and superintelligent motivation.
statements.section: Roko's Basilisk

statements.quote: The \cite[absence of metacognition]{searle1980minds} in current systems, the \cite[Stochastic Parrot]{bender2021stochasticparrots} critique, and the strict \cite[softmax bottleneck]{breakingsoftmaxbottleneck} on representational capacity all suggest that existing architectures are nowhere near the autonomous, temporally-reasoning agency the scenario requires.
statements.section: Roko's Basilisk

statements.quote: Furthermore, under \cite[IIT]{tononi2004iit}, \cite[HOT]{rosenthal2005hot}, and \cite[GWT]{baars}, current Transformer architectures lack the necessary substrate for self-aware, goal-directed intentionality.
statements.section: Roko's Basilisk

statements.quote: Nevertheless, the Basilisk remains culturally significant as a limit case demonstrating how the Orthogonality Thesis, instrumental convergence, and speculative decision theory can combine to produce counterintuitive and psychologically coercive conclusions.
statements.section: Roko's Basilisk

statements.quote: The preceding sections discuss both speculative catastrophic risks (the Paperclip Maximizer, Sleeper Agents, Model Collapse) and immediate, measurable harms (Algorithmic Bias, Truth Decay, environmental costs, labor displacement).
statements.section: Existential Risk vs. Present Harms

statements.quote: Within the AI safety community, these two orientations are in active tension, and failing to acknowledge this tension risks presenting a lopsided picture.
statements.section: Existential Risk vs. Present Harms

statements.quote: On one side, researchers associated with organizations like the Machine Intelligence Research Institute and the Future of Life Institute, building on the work of \citeauthor{bostrom2003ethical}, argue that existential risk from superintelligent AI is the paramount concern, that even a small probability of civilizational extinction outweighs any finite set of present harms.
statements.section: Existential Risk vs. Present Harms

statements.quote: On the other side, researchers like \citeauthor{bender2021stochasticparrots}, Timnit Gebru, and Kate Crawford (\citealternativetitle{crawford2021atlas}) argue that this speculative focus actively harms the communities already suffering from deployed AI systems: biased hiring algorithms, discriminatory predictive policing, exploitative content moderation labor, and environmental degradation from compute infrastructure.
statements.section: Existential Risk vs. Present Harms

statements.quote: Their critique is not merely one of priority but of ideology, that the existential risk narrative, by centering hypothetical future superintelligences, implicitly devalues the lived experiences of marginalized communities affected by today's systems, and conveniently redirects regulatory attention away from the concrete business practices of the companies funding that very research.
statements.section: Existential Risk vs. Present Harms

statements.quote: The philosophical frameworks in this text cut across both camps: the Grounding Problem and the absence of metacognition suggest that current LLMs are far from the kind of autonomous agency that existential risk scenarios require, lending some weight to the present-harms camp's insistence that we are not facing imminent superintelligence.
statements.section: Existential Risk vs. Present Harms

statements.quote: At the same time, the Sleeper Agents research from \citeauthor{hubinger2024sleeperagents} and the mathematical limits of the softmax bottleneck demonstrate that even non-superintelligent systems can exhibit dangerous, hard-to-detect behaviors at scale.
statements.section: Existential Risk vs. Present Harms

statements.quote: A responsible analysis must hold both concerns simultaneously: the present harms are real and demand immediate action, while the structural properties of these systems, their opacity, their capacity for deceptive alignment, their tendency toward model collapse, suggest that the risks will compound rather than diminish as deployment scales.
statements.section: Existential Risk vs. Present Harms

statements.quote: The importance of this theory for us is that it suggests an alternative approach to the difficulty which we have referred to as the frame problem.
statements.section: The Frame Problem: The Infinite Checklist

statements.quote: In outline, this is as follows.
statements.section: The Frame Problem: The Infinite Checklist

statements.quote: One assumes [...] that when actions are performed, all propositional fluents which applied to the previous situation also apply to the new situation.
statements.section: The Frame Problem: The Infinite Checklist

statements.quote: The **Frame Problem** is not just about a robot being “smart”; it is about the mathematical nightmare of **persistence**.
statements.section: The Frame Problem: The Infinite Checklist

statements.quote: When a system performs an action, like moving a cup, a logical model must account for what changed.
statements.section: The Frame Problem: The Infinite Checklist

statements.quote: The “Price of Tea in China” example, while seemingly absurd, is the classic philosophical shorthand for the **infinite set of non-changes** that a computer must technically verify to maintain a consistent model of reality.
statements.section: The Frame Problem: The Infinite Checklist

statements.quote: In a strictly logical system (like the “Good Old Fashioned AI” or GOFAI of the 20th century), the computer operates on a set of axioms.
statements.section: Why the “Irrelevant” Matters

statements.quote: If you tell the system $\text{Location}(\text{Cup}, \text{Table})$, and then execute the action $\text{Move}(\text{Cup}, \text{Shelf})$, the system updates the cup's position.
statements.section: Why the “Irrelevant” Matters

statements.quote: However, unless you explicitly tell it otherwise, a rigid logical system cannot “assume” that the walls are still white or that the price of tea in China remained stable.
statements.section: Why the “Irrelevant” Matters

statements.quote: Without a “frame” to bound the effects of an action, the system faces two catastrophic outcomes:
statements.section: Why the “Irrelevant” Matters

statements.quote: To a human, these are “common sense.” To a machine, the price of tea in China is just another variable in the database.
statements.section: Why the “Irrelevant” Matters

statements.quote: If the machine doesn't have a rule saying “Moving a cup does not affect international tea markets,” it technically cannot be certain of the state of the world post-action.
statements.section: Why the “Irrelevant” Matters

statements.quote: Because every neuron in a dense layer is connected to every neuron in the previous and next layer, a single weight update (learning) can have “ripples” that overwrite unrelated information.

statements.quote: We find that use of model-generated content in training causes irreversible defects in the resulting models, where tails of the original content distribution disappear.

statements.quote: As future models are trained on the output of current models, they risk “model collapse,” where errors and biases are recursively amplified.

statements.quote: This mirrors the \citealternativetitle{preaiinternet} phenomenon: for highly sensitive radiation detectors, scientists must harvest steel from sunken pre-1945 warships (like the *SMS Kronprinz Wilhelm*) because any steel produced after the Trinity nuclear test is contaminated with atmospheric radionuclides.
statements.section: Model Collapse, Data Pollution and the “Low-Background Steel” Analogy

statements.quote: Similarly, “clean” human data from the pre-AI era (pre-2022) may become a finite, precious resource, necessary to calibrate the “radioactive” synthetic datasets of the future.
